# Nomi

[![test](https://github.com/nomi-language/nomi/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/nomi-language/nomi/actions/workflows/test.yml)

Nomi is a statically typed language where every value is immutable. It has
no null and no exceptions, and a `case` must cover every shape its value can
take, so the compiler catches those mistakes before the program runs.

**[Take the tour at nomi-lang.org](https://nomi-lang.org)** to read and run Nomi
in your browser.

- **Statically typed**, with local inference: named functions spell out their
  parameters and return types; bindings and lambdas infer.
- **Bodies end in `end`**: a function, an `if`, a `case` or a type is a
  header line, its body below and `end`. Braces hold data only.
- **Fully immutable**: bindings, structs and collections are persistent;
  "modifying" returns a new value.
- **Functional-first**: first-class functions, algebraic data types,
  exhaustive `case` destructuring, and tail calls in constant stack space.
- **Explicit interfaces**: `impl Interface for Type` blocks, `derive` for
  generated implementations, and qualified calls (`Display.to_string(x)`,
  `String.length(s)`) instead of value methods.
- **Pipe-oriented**: `x |> f()` keeps data flow reading top to bottom.
- **Structured concurrency**: `concurrent` blocks, tasks, channels,
  supervisors and context-style cancellation.
- **Built-in tests**: `test` / `group` blocks and `//!` attached examples are
  ordinary Nomi code, run by `nomi test`.

Nomi compiles programs to bytecode and runs them on its own virtual machine.
The same VM runs `nomi run`, `nomi test`, the REPL, executables written by
`nomi build`, the examples in the browser tour, and Go applications that embed
Nomi. Nomi is implemented in Go, and can call Go code through a typed FFI.

## Status

Nomi is very early and pre-release. The language changes without
compatibility guarantees. The core (expressions, types, pattern matching,
imports, interfaces, derives, tests, collections and control flow) is the most
exercised; concurrency, FFI and module management are younger.

## Learn

- **[The tour](https://nomi-lang.org/introduction/)**: the language a chapter
  at a time, with examples that run in the browser.
  [First Steps](https://nomi-lang.org/learn/values/) is for someone new to
  programming, and [Coming from…](https://nomi-lang.org/coming-from/) has a
  guide for each of several languages.
- **[The cheat sheet](docs/cheatsheet.md)**: the rules most often written
  wrong, with checked examples.
- **[The language spec](docs/spec.md)**: canonical for what the language
  does.
- **[The tooling reference](docs/tooling.md)**: the `nomi` command,
  `nomi.toml`, dependencies, the test runner and builds.
- **[Style guide](docs/style.md)**, **[feature status](docs/feature-status.md)**,
  **[roadmap](docs/roadmap.md)**.

## Getting started

You need git and Go 1.21 or newer. If your Go is older than the version Nomi
builds with, the first build downloads that version for you.

Clone the repository and install `nomi` and the language server `nomi lsp`:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/nomi-language/nomi.git
cd nomi
go install ./cmd/nomi ./cmd/nomi lsp
```

`go install` puts both in `$(go env GOPATH)/bin` (usually `~/go/bin`); make
sure that directory is on your `PATH`. Keep the checkout: editor support is
installed from it. [`docs/install.md`](docs/install.md) covers the rest,
including `go install ...@latest` without a clone.

Write a first program in a directory of your own, outside the checkout. Save
this as `~/hello-nomi/hello.nomi`:

```nomi
import std::io

fn main()
    io.print("Hello, Nomi!")
end
```
```sh
cd ~/hello-nomi
nomi run hello.nomi        # prints Hello, Nomi!
nomi                       # or try expressions in the REPL
```

Then set up your editor from [Editor support](#editor-support) below.

## Usage

```sh
nomi run app.nomi                          # run a program
./app.nomi a b                             # run a file whose first line is #!/usr/bin/env nomi
nomi test                                  # run every test under the current directory
nomi                                       # an interactive REPL
nomi build app.nomi                        # write a standalone executable
nomi build app.nomi --target linux/amd64   # ... for another platform
nomi build app.nomi --target wasip1/wasm   # ... as a WebAssembly module
nomi build app.nomi --web                  # write app-web/, a page that runs it in a browser,
                                           # with the files of web/ beside it copied in
nomi run --web app.nomi                    # serve that page and web/ on localhost; reload it on every edit
nomi build app.nomi --no-vm                # write app.nomic, the compiled program alone, for any platform's nomi-vm
nomi build-vm                              # write nomi-vm, which runs a compiled program it is given:
nomi-vm app.nomic a b                      #   by path, or
cat app.nomic input | nomi-vm              #   framed on stdin, the rest being the program's input
nomi check app.nomi                        # type-check without running
nomi fmt -w .                              # format
```

## Editor support

Every editor launches `nomi lsp` from `PATH`. Helix, Neovim and Zed parse with
the tree-sitter grammar in [`tree-sitter-nomi/`](tree-sitter-nomi/); VS Code
and bat highlight with regex grammars instead (VS Code's is derived from
bat's). The tree-sitter grammar is also published read-only at
[nomi-language/tree-sitter-nomi](https://github.com/nomi-language/tree-sitter-nomi).
Run each command from the repository root, and again after `git pull`. The
Helix and Neovim setups compile the grammar, so they need `make`, `python3`
and a C compiler (on macOS, the Xcode Command Line Tools:
`xcode-select --install`).

| Editor | Directory | Setup |
|---|---|---|
| Helix | [`editors/helix/`](editors/helix/) | `make install-helix`. It ends with `hx --health nomi`, which should find the parser, the queries, `nomi lsp` and the `nomi` formatter. Its README has the manual route. |
| Neovim 0.11+ | [`editors/nvim/`](editors/nvim/) | `make install-nvim`. Its README covers lazy.nvim. |
| VS Code | [`editors/vscode/`](editors/vscode/) | `make install-vscode`, which needs Node 22+ and npm. It builds `editors/vscode/nomi.vsix` and installs it with `code`; its README has the details. |
| Zed | [`editors/zed/`](editors/zed/) | `scripts/sync-zed-grammar.sh`, then run "zed: install dev extension" in Zed and select `editors/zed/`. Zed compiles the extension, which needs Rust installed through rustup. |
| bat (and syntect users) | [`editors/bat/`](editors/bat/) | See its README. |

Helix, Neovim, VS Code and Zed draw attached tests (`//!` lines) dimmed, so they do
not compete with the code they test; their diagnostics are drawn at full
strength. Neovim and VS Code show the attached test under the cursor normally
(their READMEs have the settings). In Zed, if you turn semantic tokens on, the
extension's `semantic_token_rules.json` keeps their identifiers dimmed too.

VS Code, Neovim, Zed and Helix debug Nomi through `nomi dap`, a Debug Adapter
Protocol server: breakpoints with conditions, hit counts and logpoints,
stepping, the call stack, locals, each pipeline stage's value, watches, hovers
and a debug console that evaluate Nomi in the paused frame, restart frame,
function breakpoints, step into target, go to a variable's binding, and step
back and reverse continue (by replaying the program with the input, clock and
randomness it recorded), for a program's `main` or a single test. VS Code
and Neovim put a Debug lens beside each Run lens; VS Code needs nothing more, and Neovim needs
[nvim-dap](https://github.com/mfussenegger/nvim-dap). Zed's extension
registers the adapter and gives each `nomi run` and `nomi test` task a debug
entry. Helix's `languages.toml` block adds run and test templates to
`:debug-start`. The VS Code and Neovim READMEs have the launch settings.

Each editor also attaches `nomi lsp` to a module's `nomi.toml`, for the
errors `nomi check` reports there and completion in its `[effects]`
lists, and to its phrase catalogs, the TOML files under its
`[i18n].catalogs` directory (`locales/` unless the manifest names another),
for their diagnostics, completion, hover and quick fixes. The file keeps
the editor's TOML highlighting. VS Code and Neovim attach to every
`nomi.toml`, and read each one to attach to its module's catalogs only.
Helix's `languages.toml` adds a `nomi-catalog` language for `nomi.toml` and
`locales/**/*.toml`, using Helix's TOML grammar. Zed attaches a server by
language, not by path, so the server is sent every TOML buffer and responds
only for a `nomi.toml` and catalogs; `"languages": { "TOML": {
"language_servers": ["!nomi lsp", "..."] } }` turns that off.

Comments wrap at 100 columns, `nomi fmt`'s line width. Neovim sets
`textwidth=100`, so a comment breaks as you type and `gw` reflows it (`gq`
goes to the formatter in most LSP setups, and `nomi fmt` leaves comments
alone), and
Helix sets `text-width = 100` for `:reflow`. A Zed extension cannot set a
line length, so add it to your Zed settings for "editor: rewrap":
`"languages": { "Nomi": { "preferred_line_length": 100 } }`.

To work on Nomi itself, run `make dev-editors` instead. It installs `nomi` and
`nomi lsp` from the checkout and makes each installed editor read the
checkout: Helix's queries are linked rather than copied, Neovim loads
`editors/nvim` through lazy.nvim with a parser compiled beside it, and it says
when Zed's dev extension needs reinstalling.

## Contributing

Nomi is not accepting pull requests yet. The language and compiler still
change too quickly for an outside change to land without being reworked, and
that isn't a fair use of a contributor's time. Bug reports, questions and
feedback are welcome as [issues](https://github.com/nomi-language/nomi/issues).

To build and test from source, see [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](CONTRIBUTING.md) and
[`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md).

markdown:
# Contributing to Nomi

Nomi is not accepting pull requests yet. The language and compiler still
change too quickly for an outside change to land without being reworked.
Bug reports, questions and feedback are welcome as
[issues](https://github.com/nomi-language/nomi/issues). The rest of this file
is how to build and test Nomi from source.

Nomi is early and pre-release. The language changes freely, with no
compatibility promise yet, so expect breaking changes and prefer the better
design over the backward-compatible one.

[`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md) is the full working guide to this repository
(architecture, verification cadence, grammar workflow, conventions). It is
written for human contributors and coding agents alike. This file is the short
version.

## Prerequisites

- Go (the version on the `go` line of `go.mod`; with `GOTOOLCHAIN=auto` an
  older Go downloads it).
- For the tour site: Node 22 or newer.
- For grammar work: Node (for the tree-sitter CLI via `npx`); for the Zed
  extension build, Rust with the `wasm32-wasip2` target.

## Build

```sh
go build -o nomi ./cmd/nomi   # the CLI, at ./nomi (gitignored)
go install ./cmd/nomi         # `nomi` on your PATH
go install ./cmd/nomi lsp     # the language server
```

## Test

```sh
go test ./... -count=1         # compiler, VM, LSP, runtime library
go test ./rt/... -count=1      # the runtime library on its own
./nomi test tests
./nomi test std
```

The VM's output is checked against golden files in
`testdata/expectations/`. If your change moves one, regenerate it
(the command is in AGENTS.md) and say why each record moved in the commit
message.

## Format

Run `nomi fmt -w <paths>` on any `.nomi` file you edit, and `gofmt` on Go
files.

## Where things are written down

- [Language spec](docs/spec.md): canonical for what
  the language does. Update it in the same change as the feature.
- [Style guide](docs/style.md): how to write idiomatic Nomi.
- [Feature status](docs/feature-status.md): aspirational spec
  sections, gaps, tooling capabilities and known defects.
- [Roadmap](docs/roadmap.md): the larger work ahead.
- [Tour](tour/): the documentation site; see its README to run
  it locally.

## Changes

Keep each commit one coherent change with its tests. Describe what changed
and why in the commit message. For a change to the grammar, follow the
checklist in AGENTS.md: the grammar feeds the Zed, Helix, Neovim and bat
syntax definitions, and the tour's grammar wasm.

## Releases

Pushing a `v*` tag runs `.github/workflows/release.yml`, which runs
`scripts/release.sh <tag>` and attaches its output to a GitHub release. The
script can be run by hand too:

```sh
./scripts/release.sh v0.1.0
```

It writes `dist/nomi_<version>_<os>_<arch>.{tar.gz,zip}` and
`dist/nomi_<version>_checksums.txt` (`NOMI_RELEASE_DIST=<dir>` writes them
elsewhere, for a dry run). The version must be the release's tag: it is
stamped into `nomi` (`-X github.com/nomi-language/nomi/internal/ffirun.ReleaseVersion=<version>`), and
`nomi build --target` downloads other platforms' nomi-vm from that tag. The
script reads each binary's platform and commit back with `go version -m` and
fails if they disagree with the target or with each other.

## License

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally
submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0
license, shall be dual licensed as in [README.md](README.md#license), without
any additional terms or conditions.

# Installing Nomi

Nomi is pre-release and changes from day to day, so most people should build
it from a clone: that is where editor support is installed from, and `git
pull` keeps it current. `go install github.com/nomi-language/nomi/cmd/nomi@latest`
builds the newest commit on `main` without a clone. No versions are tagged
and no prebuilt binaries are published yet. Set up an editor from a clone
either way (see the [README](../README.md#editor-support)).

## From source

You need git and Go 1.21 or newer. If your Go is older than the version Nomi
builds with, the first build downloads that version for you, unless you have
set `GOTOOLCHAIN=local`.

```console
$ git clone https://github.com/nomi-language/nomi.git
$ go install -C nomi ./cmd/nomi ./cmd/nomi lsp
$ nomi --version
```

On a Mac with Xcode's command line tools, `nomi` starts about 1 ms faster
linked by the system linker, which `make build` and `make dev-editors` do:

```console
$ CGO_ENABLED=1 go install -C nomi -ldflags=-linkmode=external ./cmd/nomi ./cmd/nomi lsp
```

`go install` writes `nomi` and `nomi lsp` to `$(go env GOPATH)/bin`, usually
`~/go/bin`, which must be on `PATH`. Editors find the language server as
`nomi lsp` and the debugger as `nomi dap`, so these two binaries are all an
editor needs from the install (Neovim also needs the nvim-dap plugin to
debug). A source build's `nomi --version` prints
the commit, with `-dirty` appended when the checkout had uncommitted changes:

```console
nomi 0123456789ab (go1.27.0 darwin/arm64)
```

Keep the checkout where it is. A `nomi` built from a clone is a development
build: `nomi build` and `nomi build-vm` build nomi-vm from the checkout, and a project with Go
bindings compiles against it. To point a development build at another

checkout's root. The variable also makes a `go install`ed `nomi` build Go
bindings against a checkout instead of its own version, which is how to try
compiler changes on a project without reinstalling.

## With `go install`

With Go 1.21 or newer, install without cloning:

```console
$ go install github.com/nomi-language/nomi/cmd/nomi@latest github.com/nomi-language/nomi/cmd/nomi lsp@latest
```

names another one. `nomi --version` prints the module's pseudo-version.

This `nomi` needs no checkout. A project with Go bindings compiles against the
compiler module at `nomi`'s own version, which the Go toolchain fetches into
the module cache like any other dependency, through your `GOPROXY` and
checksum database. `go install` installs no `nomi-vm`, so `nomi build` and

caches it. The executable `nomi build` writes needs nothing installed.

A release archive's `nomi` (once releases are published) and a `go
install`ed one need nothing else for a project without Go bindings, its
dependencies included: `nomi` fetches the modules `go.mod` requires through
the Go module proxy itself (`nomi add`, `nomi fetch`). `nomi new` starts a
project (`nomi init` makes an existing directory one), and `nomi` writes its

Any other project with Go bindings, its own or a dependency's, is built with

yourself. The editor's language server never downloads modules or Go: run
`nomi fetch` in the project once, which downloads everything the project
needs, so the editor finds every module and `--offline` commands need no
network. Go bindings build without cgo, so a Go package that calls C cannot
be bound.

## Windows

Nomi builds for Windows (amd64) and has not yet been run there. Every
package cross-compiles, and CI has Windows jobs that run the whole test
suite, which have not reported yet; treat Windows as untested. The commands
above are the same in PowerShell, and install `nomi.exe` and
`nomi lsp.exe` to `%USERPROFILE%\go\bin`. Set Git's `core.autocrlf` to
`false` before cloning if you will run the tests, since their recorded
output has LF line ends; Nomi itself reads source with either.

Where Windows differs:

- `nomi build` with no `-o` writes `<entry>.exe`.
- The managed Go toolchain is kept in `%LocalAppData%\nomi\go`.
- Paths in a Nomi program use `/`, and std::fs also takes `\`; a drive is
  `C:/Users`.
- The debugger's integrated terminal needs Windows 10 version 1803 or later
  (it connects over a Unix socket).

# Nomi Roadmap: Big-Ticket Items

The strategic punch list of large, cross-cutting initiatives: the things that
take a design pass and several changes. It complements:

- [`spec.md`](spec.md), the canonical spec for what the language does.
- [`feature-status.md`](feature-status.md), the aspirational-spec punch list, gaps in shipped features, tooling capabilities and known defects.

This file is the forward view: open work only. When an item lands, delete it here; the spec says what works, and feature-status.md lists what the item left unbuilt.

## The organizing principle

Sort by retrofit cost: how expensive a thing is to change after code depends
on it.

1. **There is one engine.** The front end (parse, analyze, type-check) feeds
   `internal/irbuild`, which lowers every body to IR; the VM compiles that IR to
   bytecode and runs it over `rt`'s values. `nomi run`, `nomi test`, the REPL,
   the tour, `nomi build`'s executables and Go embedders all use it. Golden
   files under `testdata/expectations/` are the only oracle.
2. **Irreversible semantics before additive features.** A numeric, string or
   collection decision baked into every program matters more than any feature
   that can be added later without breaking anyone.

## Track 1: Execution and tooling

- [ ] **Stdlib startup cost.** A built `nomi` runs hello world with no program record (std artifact, bundle and state warm in the artifact cache) in a median of 28 ms of wall time on an Apple M2 Max shared with other work (load average 5 to 9), from 44 ms; a Go binary that only prints starts and exits in 3.5 ms under the same harness. The stdlib's base modules (the prelude, std/assertions and std/io with what they import, 54 of 101) are no longer built: a process reads them back from a state the previous process wrote beside the artifact, their facts installed and their `StdBase` formed (the analysis package doc, "The stdlib's state"), and reads each file's kept declarations only when a module's bodies are checked. A binary built with `nomi_stdbundle` (a release, the tour's wasm) embeds the state, which `stdbundlegen` writes in a process of its own and keys by the artifact and a digest of the generated codecs, so it reads it on its first run: a release-style hello world in an empty cache takes 32 ms against 48 ms, and the tour's wasm starts in about 149 ms against 230 ms under node (the state's decode there is 80 ms), for 0.7 MB more gzipped wasm. Keeping the program record writes the file record beside the load record and walks the lowering for undefined linkage names on four goroutines. Where the 28 ms go: 9.2 ms from spawn to `main`, from 9.8 (a trivial Go binary reaches its `main` at 3.3 ms; see below), the state's decode 7.1 ms (16 MB, 74k objects), the rest of the std setup 1.8 ms (the artifact read, the state file read), the program's own front end 2.2 ms, its lowering 2 ms (most of it restoring the bundle's modules), keeping the program record 2.6 ms, `main` 0.3 ms and exit 1.3 ms. The target of 10 ms from the process's start to `main` returning is not met: that span is now about 17 ms. Next: the decode is allocation-bound (the symbols, the AST nodes and the position-keyed maps), so a smaller state is the lever: the builders and per-file copies a file keeps for rebuilding its bodies are already deferred, and the position maps could be kept as sorted slices; the bundle's module restore could be kept the same way; a program reaching further modules still builds them with the sweeps over the read-back base (about 3 ms each) and forms their `StdBase` again (5 ms); and the listed modules' kept lowering is decoded whole, so a program reaching one listed module builds all of them (the HTTP chapter's first block builds 96 modules). Before `main`, a time profile of 300 launches splits `nomi`'s CPU as: dyld applying 160k rebase fixups 32% (the Go linker writes them as 884 KB of rebase opcodes, 112k of them in type descriptors); the initializers of the 350 system images that Security and CoreFoundation pull in 18% (crypto/x509 links both on macOS, and a Go binary that imports only crypto/x509 reaches `main` 1.4 ms after one that does not); dyld's loading 11%; package inits 11% (1.2 ms by `GODEBUG=inittrace=1`, from 2.0 ms; the largest left are encoding/gob, BurntSushi/toml's internal package, x/crypto/ssh through commonlog and go-dap, 0.3 ms together, none of them nomi's); the Go runtime 8%; and the kernel's exec, page faults and exit the rest. The binary's size costs little on its own: its 59 MB are 17.6 MB of code, a 13.2 MB pclntab, 13.6 MB of DWARF (not mapped at launch; stripping it changes nothing), 3.2 MB of type descriptors, 3.8 MB of CLDR data and 1.8 MB of std sources, and nothing reads the data before `main`. Linking with the system linker (`CGO_ENABLED=1 -ldflags=-linkmode=external`) writes chained fixups instead: `nomi version` takes 8.7 ms against 9.9 and hello world 27.4 against 28.4. `make build` and `make dev-editors` link `nomi` and `nomi lsp` so on a Mac with Xcode's command line tools; Go 1.27's own linker cannot write chained fixups. Releases keep Go's linker: external linking needs cgo and a C linker for the target, and they are cross-built with CGO_ENABLED=0 on one Linux runner, so a darwin release linked so would need a macOS runner. A built executable gains nothing measurable (its `nomi-vm-nonet` runner has 36k rebases, not 160k; 5.7 ms either way), so runners stay on Go's linker. One cut is left there: a `nomi` that did not link crypto/x509 would save about 1.4 ms, which means a separate binary for programs and commands that reach the network.
- [ ] **Incremental compilation, what remains.** The language server checks incrementally in memory (`internal/analysis/recheck.go`, `recheck_dependents.go`), opens a project from a record of its files' interfaces, facts, references and the entry's kept lowering (`stored_program.go`), and takes edits in a program opened so (`stored_edit.go`, `stored_inplace.go`, `stored_lowering.go`, `stored_refs.go`); `nomi run`, `check`, `test` and `build` relink a kept program from its file records (`vmhost/filerecord.go`). At 50k generated lines (221 files) the first body edit after an open from a record takes 8 to 34 ms, references to a function 137 files call 0.12 s, and the entry's lowering after a body edit 0.28 s. What remains. A program with Go bindings keeps no record: the server builds each of its documents on its own and keeps no program for it, so moving such projects onto kept programs comes first. An edit that leaves something to report is taken from the record unless it is a diagnostic only the program checked whole words (an impl collision or orphan, a missing impl, a reduction's diagnostic in a file the edit does not check again), or the program has an application type. In a program with an application type, an edit that changes the walk its application-field roots take of a checked file's bodies (a new call, a read added or moved into a lambda) checks the whole program: the walk follows calls into other files' bodies (`appReadWalker.contained`, interface default methods, every impl of a dispatched method), and its alias and inspection state carry from one file's body into the next, so per-file facts would have to hold each executing expression with its resolved reference and replay the walker over them; the server compares each checked file's walk summary instead (`AppWalkSummary`), which a positions-only edit keeps. `nomi check`'s relink from file records compares the same summaries. The language server checks an edit that reaches more than 16 files and a quarter of the program (a hub's signature) whole, and that stays: at 50k lines the hub's signature reaches 210 of 221 files, each of whose checks against interfaces builds the hub's interface and its own closure (opening a leaf from a record costs about 10 ms, so 2.1 s for 210), and each file's lowering links against every other's, where the whole check takes 1.03 s.
- [ ] **Debugger follow-ups.** The debugger plan has landed (feature-status's *Debugger* section). Left: attaching to a running process or a `nomi build` executable (the image keeps the debug info); debugging a program with Go bindings, which runs in a generated wrapper process; and step back in a program with more than one task, which a replay cannot reproduce without recording the scheduler's choices too.
- [ ] **The builder's `mobile` flag.** The builder's `lower` still returns whether a value may be read more than once without a copy, and about a hundred call sites pass it on. The VM evaluates each temporary once, so the flag and the `irCopyForce` copies it guards could go. It is a large mechanical change with no behaviour behind it.
- [ ] **FFI follow-ups.**
  - Runtime-typed dispatch (an `import_impls` escape hatch) for values from FFI or deserialization whose impls the analyzer cannot record statically.
  - `host type` field access and Nomi-side construction.
- [ ] **A prebuilt `nomi` still needs Go for Go FFI beyond lib/.** A release runs, tests and builds a project whose bindings are all the first-party lib/ modules' at its commit on prebuilt binaries from a lib archive (`internal/ffirun/libprebuilt.go`). Any other Go binding, a lib/ module at another commit, a `wasip1/wasm` build of a lib/ project and a program importing `std::compiler` still build a wrapper or a nomi-vm with Go; without Go they refuse naming what needs it. No release has been cut with the lib archives yet, so the download path is tested only against a local server. Homebrew and Scoop packages are not written: they need a tap and a bucket repository.
- [ ] **Standalone WASM programs, what remains.** `nomi build --target js/wasm` and `--target wasip1/wasm` write valid modules, and the wasip1 ones need no file access. A hello world is 11 MB (2.0 MB brotli) and starts in about 130 ms under Node, most of it compiling the module. Browser use is checked by hand in Chromium only: `nomi build --web` pages, a cached wasip1 `nomi-vm` running `.nomic` programs framed on stdin through `@bjorn3/browser_wasi_shim`, and `nomi-wasi.js` loading and running programs in the reactor. The automated tests drive all of these under Node; Firefox and Safari are untried. wasmtime has run a command module; the reactor has not been tried there. GC behaviour is unmeasured. `--web` links a project's Go bindings into `app.wasm` (tested under Node; a bound package that does not build for js/wasm is refused at its `gopkg`), refuses file access where a `files` option served from the worker's `fs` could stand in, and has no `nomi test` counterpart.
- [ ] **Link only the Go code a program reaches, beyond the network.** `nomi build` appends a program that reaches no network crossing to a runner built without net/http, crypto/tls and net (`nomi-vm-nonet`, about a third smaller, which reaches `main` in 5.1 ms against `nomi-vm`'s 7.1 ms on macOS, most of the difference the Security framework crypto/x509 links). The rest of std's Go side (CLDR formatting, collation, regex, processes) is still linked into every runner; linking each program's runner from the crossings it reaches, as Go-FFI projects' runners are, would cut every target further. A browser client that calls `fetch` through `syscall/js` without `http.Client` would cut a program that does use std::http by about 4.5 MB.
- [ ] **Calling JavaScript from Nomi.** A page calls a Nomi program's exported functions (`nomi.js`'s `load` and `call`), but Nomi cannot call the page: no DOM, `fetch` or local storage. The mirror of `export fn` would be a small set of host functions in a `std::web`-like module, or the page passing callbacks to `load`. Nothing is designed.
- [ ] **An npm package for the wasm build** (`cmd/nomi-wasm`, the tour's runtime) with a small JS API: run source, hover, semantic tokens.
- [ ] **Tour hardening, what remains.** The stack-depth limit (`rt/calldepth_js.go`, 1,000 calls) and the run-worker's recovery were measured in Chrome and Node only; Firefox and Safari are unmeasured. And a Go fatal error prints a goroutine trace to the worker's console naming the build machine's paths; `-trimpath` would remove them, and it must go on both `scripts/build-tour-wasm.sh` and `vmhost/tour_bundle_test.go`'s rebuild at once.
- [ ] **Doc-gen, registry and package-manager UX.** `nomi doc`, publishing, distribution polish. Nomi modules ride the Go module proxy.
  - `nomi publish` is reserved. Publishing a module is pushing a version tag to its repository, as for any Go module, and the module proxy serves it from there.
  - A registry. There is no Nomi-specific registry, and none is planned; if Nomi-specific module discovery becomes a need, the simplest path is metadata indexing on top of existing Go module hosting rather than a parallel registry.
  - Compiler-enforced semver: a compiler that diffs the public API between versions and rejects mismatched version bumps. A long-horizon nice-to-have. The closest existing precedent is Elm/Gleam; the mechanism requires both a registry hook (where to compare against) and a published-API extraction step that doesn't exist yet.

## Track 2: Irreversible semantics

- [ ] **Language versioning and compatibility.** The mechanism (editions, fixers, a compatibility promise) for when the language stops breaking. Until then it breaks freely, which is correct before a first release.
- [ ] **Exhaustive struct pattern opt-in.** Struct pattern matching is partial by default: unmentioned fields are ignored. A `!..` marker could opt into exhaustive field matching, so `User{name:, age:, email:, !..}` would become a compile error when `User` gains a field. This is the inverse of Rust, where `..` opts *out* of exhaustive matching. It waits on real usage showing the need.

## Track 3: Architecture to leave room for

- [ ] **A stable serialization format.** The linked-IR image (`ir.EncodeImage`/`DecodeImage`) is the one serialized form today and carries no compatibility promise outside `.nomic`, which `ir.FormatVersion` versions. An object is the same format: one module encoded alone, whose symbols carry their linkage names, so objects, instances and images share one codec and one version. Front-end artifacts have a codec of their own beside it: a file's interface (`analysis.FileInterface`) writes its declarations' nodes with `internal/ast/astcodec`, generated from the AST's types, under its own version.
- [ ] **WASM Component Model interop** for cross-language imports and exports. WIT interfaces and `wasip2` components are the standard that would replace the wasip1 reactor's generic `nomi_call` ABI, which passes function names and JSON as data because one prebuilt runner serves every program and Go fixes a module's export names when it links it. Go cannot produce components yet. Track it; nothing is designed.

## Track 4: Big but additive

- [ ] **Unified container type/value syntax.** Tuples (`(Int, String)` ↔ `(1, "x")`) and anonymous structs (`{a: Int}` ↔ `{a: 1}`) already use one outer syntax for type and value; lists and maps do not (`List<Int>` vs `[1, 2, 3]`). Proposal: also accept `[Int]` and `{String => Int}` as type forms. Needs its own design.
- [ ] **Field-projection derive** (`derive Getters for T`). For an interface whose functions are pure field projections (`fn hour(value: self) -> Int`), synthesize the trivial impl, which would remove boilerplate like `std::calendar`'s `DateParts`/`TimeParts` impls. `derive` covers `Equatable`, `Hashable`, `Comparable`, `Debug`, `Display`, `ToJson` and `FromJson` today.
- [ ] **Opaque handles for exported functions.** Every argument and result of an `export fn` crosses as JSON, so a value the host passes back unchanged is encoded and decoded on each call. A handle (a value that stays in the VM, referred to by an id) would matter for large values and values with no JSON form. Wait for a program that needs it.
- [ ] **Checked examples in stdlib `///` comments.** The generated reference renders a declaration's `//!` attached tests as runnable editors, and those are the stdlib's examples. A ` ```nomi ` block inside a `///` comment is only highlighted: nothing parses, checks or runs it, so one can go stale unnoticed. Either check those blocks or settle that `//!` is the only example form.

## Track 5: Standard library I/O and services

Where each item lives follows one rule. std holds what Go's standard library can back with no third-party code: `std::fs`, `std::sql`'s vocabulary, later `std::http` over `net/http`. `lib/` holds first-party modules that need third-party Go code or are opinionated layers over std: database drivers (`lib/sql/sqlite`), `lib/sql/sqlkit`, later an HTTP router or framework. Each `lib/` module is its own module with its own `go.mod`, versioned with nomi's commits, tested by nomi's checks, and added by users with `nomi add github.com/nomi-language/nomi/lib/...`.

What a program needs to talk to the world outside the VM. The items are in the agreed order. Items 1 and 2 and the subprocesses `std::process` now has share one stream type (`Reader`/`Writer`) and one test seam, and were designed together in the I/O design proposal (`docs/design/io.md`, not committed), which also sketches 3, 4, 5 and 7. Every item is backed by Go's standard library, so no program needs a Go toolchain to use it.

- [ ] **2. The file system, the rest.** `std::fs`, `std::path` and `std::fs::testing` exist (whole files with a `WriteMode`, lines and chunks, streams, directories, walks and globs, metadata, symlinks and modes, `io.File` with reads and writes at a position, `fs.within` over `os.Root`, temporary directories, an in-memory sandbox, a conformance suite, the browser's in-memory file system). Missing: a test group line that seals a test's real file calls. Paths use `/` on every system, Windows hosts accepting `\` too.
- [ ] **5. HTTP under Node.** `std::http`, `std::tls` and `std::net` cover Go's HTTP packages (the `internal/stdhttp` package doc; `internal/stdhttp/inventory.txt` names each of Go's identifiers and what Nomi does with it). Missing: a js/wasm request run under Node, where Go's transport does not use `fetch`.

Next: the decode is allocation-bound (the symbols, the AST nodes and the position-keyed maps), so a smaller state is the lever: the builders and per-file copies a file keeps for rebuilding its bodies are already deferred, and the position maps could be kept as sorted slices; the bundle's module restore could be kept the same way; a program reaching further modules still builds them with the sweeps over the read-back base (about 3 ms each) and forms their StdBase again (5 ms); and the listed modules' kept lowering is decoded whole, so a program reaching one listed module builds all of them (the HTTP chapter's first block builds 96 modules). Before main, a time profile of 300 launches splits nomi's CPU as: dyld applying 160k rebase fixups 32% (the Go linker writes them as 884 KB of rebase opcodes, 112k of them in type descriptors); the initializers of the 350 system images that Security and CoreFoundation pull in 18% (crypto/x509 links both on macOS, and a Go binary that imports only crypto/x509 reaches main 1.4 ms after one that does not); dyld's loading 11%; package inits 11% (1.2 ms by GODEBUG=inittrace=1, from 2.0 ms; the largest left are encoding/gob, BurntSushi/toml's internal package, x/crypto/ssh through commonlog and go-dap, 0.3 ms together, none of them nomi's); the Go runtime 8%; and the kernel's exec, page faults and exit the rest. The binary's size costs little on its own: its 59 MB are 17.6 MB of code, a 13.2 MB pclntab, 13.6 MB of DWARF (not mapped at launch; stripping it changes nothing), 3.2 MB of type descriptors, 3.8 MB of CLDR data and 1.8 MB of std sources, and nothing reads the data before main. Linking with the system linker (CGO_ENABLED=1 -ldflags=-linkmode=external) writes chained fixups instead: nomi version takes 8.7 ms against 9.9 and hello world 27.4 against 28.4. make build and make dev-editors link nomi and nomi lsp so on a Mac with Xcode's command line tools; Go 1.27's own linker cannot write chained fixups. Releases keep Go's linker: external linking needs cgo and a C linker for the target, and they are cross-built with CGO_ENABLED=0 on one Linux runner, so a darwin release linked so would need a macOS runner. A built executable gains nothing measurable (its nomi-vm-nonet runner has 36k rebases, not 160k; 5.7 ms either way), so runners stay on Go's linker. One cut is left there: a nomi that did not link crypto/x509 would save about 1.4 ms, which means a separate binary for programs and commands that reach the network.
  • Incremental compilation, what remains. The language server checks incrementally in memory (internal/analysis/recheck.go, recheck_dependents.go), opens a project from a record of its files' interfaces, facts, references and the entry's kept lowering (stored_program.go), and takes edits in a program opened so (stored_edit.go, stored_inplace.go, stored_lowering.go, stored_refs.go); nomi run, check, test and build relink a kept program from its file records (vmhost/filerecord.go). At 50k generated lines (221 files) the first body edit after an open from a record takes 8 to 34 ms, references to a function 137 files call 0.12 s, and the entry's lowering after a body edit 0.28 s. What remains. A program with Go bindings keeps no record: the server builds each of its documents on its own and keeps no program for it, so moving such projects onto kept programs comes first. An edit that leaves something to report is taken from the record unless it is a diagnostic only the program checked whole words (an impl collision or orphan, a missing impl, a reduction's diagnostic in a file the edit does not check again), or the program has an application type. In a program with an application type, an edit that changes the walk its application-field roots take of a checked file's bodies (a new call, a read added or moved into a lambda) checks the whole program: the walk follows calls into other files' bodies (appReadWalker.contained, interface default methods, every impl of a dispatched method), and its alias and inspection state carry from one file's body into the next, so per-file facts would have to hold each executing expression with its resolved reference and replay the walker over them; the server compares each checked file's walk summary instead (AppWalkSummary), which a positions-only edit keeps. nomi check's relink from file records compares the same summaries. The language server checks an edit that reaches more than 16 files and a quarter of the program (a hub's signature) whole, and that stays: at 50k lines the hub's signature reaches 210 of 221 files, each of whose checks against interfaces builds the hub's interface and its own closure (opening a leaf from a record costs about 10 ms, so 2.1 s for 210), and each file's lowering links against every other's, where the whole check takes 1.03 s.
  • Debugger follow-ups. The debugger plan has landed (feature-status's Debugger section). Left: attaching to a running process or a nomi build executable (the image keeps the debug info); debugging a program with Go bindings, which runs in a generated wrapper process; and step back in a program with more than one task, which a replay cannot reproduce without recording the scheduler's choices too.
  • The builder's mobile flag. The builder's lower still returns whether a value may be read more than once without a copy, and about a hundred call sites pass it on. The VM evaluates each temporary once, so the flag and the irCopyForce copies it guards could go. It is a large mechanical change with no behaviour behind it.
  • FFI follow-ups.
    • Runtime-typed dispatch (an import_impls escape hatch) for values from FFI or deserialization whose impls the analyzer cannot record statically.
    • host type field access and Nomi-side construction.
  • A prebuilt nomi still needs Go for Go FFI beyond lib/. A release runs, tests and builds a project whose bindings are all the first-party lib/ modules' at its commit on prebuilt binaries from a lib archive (internal/ffirun/libprebuilt.go). Any other Go binding, a lib/ module at another commit, a wasip1/wasm build of a lib/ project and a program importing std::compiler still build a wrapper or a nomi-vm with Go; without Go they refuse naming what needs it. No release has been cut with the lib archives yet, so the download path is tested only against a local server. Homebrew and Scoop packages are not written: they need a tap and a bucket repository.
  • Standalone WASM programs, what remains. nomi build --target js/wasm and --target wasip1/wasm write valid modules, and the wasip1 ones need no file access. A hello world is 11 MB (2.0 MB brotli) and starts in about 130 ms under Node, most of it compiling the module. Browser use is checked by hand in Chromium only: nomi build --web pages, a cached wasip1 nomi-vm running .nomic programs framed on stdin through @bjorn3/browser_wasi_shim, and nomi-wasi.js loading and running programs in the reactor. The automated tests drive all of these under Node; Firefox and Safari are untried. wasmtime has run a command module; the reactor has not been tried there. GC behaviour is unmeasured. --web links a project's Go bindings into app.wasm (tested under Node; a bound package that does not build for js/wasm is refused at its gopkg), refuses file access where a files option served from the worker's fs could stand in, and has no nomi test counterpart.
  • Link only the Go code a program reaches, beyond the network. nomi build appends a program that reaches no network crossing to a runner built without net/http, crypto/tls and net (nomi-vm-nonet, about a third smaller, which reaches main in 5.1 ms against nomi-vm's 7.1 ms on macOS, most of the difference the Security framework crypto/x509 links). The rest of std's Go side (CLDR formatting, collation, regex, processes) is still linked into every runner; linking each program's runner from the crossings it reaches, as Go-FFI projects' runners are, would cut every target further. A browser client that calls fetch through syscall/js without http.Client would cut a program that does use std::http by about 4.5 MB.
  • Calling JavaScript from Nomi. A page calls a Nomi program's exported functions (nomi.js's load and call), but Nomi cannot call the page: no DOM, fetch or local storage. The mirror of export fn would be a small set of host functions in a std::web-like module, or the page passing callbacks to load. Nothing is designed.
  • An npm package for the wasm build (cmd/nomi-wasm, the tour's runtime) with a small JS API: run source, hover, semantic tokens.
  • Tour hardening, what remains. The stack-depth limit (rt/calldepth_js.go, 1,000 calls) and the run-worker's recovery were measured in Chrome and Node only; Firefox and Safari are unmeasured. And a Go fatal error prints a goroutine trace to the worker's console naming the build machine's paths; -trimpath would remove them, and it must go on both scripts/build-tour-wasm.sh and vmhost/tour_bundle_test.go's rebuild at once.
  • Doc-gen, registry and package-manager UX. nomi doc, publishing, distribution polish. Nomi modules ride the Go module proxy.
    • nomi publish is reserved. Publishing a module is pushing a version tag to its repository, as for any Go module, and the module proxy serves it from there.
    • A registry. There is no Nomi-specific registry, and none is planned; if Nomi-specific module discovery becomes a need, the simplest path is metadata indexing on top of existing Go module hosting rather than a parallel registry.
    • Compiler-enforced semver: a compiler that diffs the public API between versions and rejects mismatched version bumps. A long-horizon nice-to-have. The closest existing precedent is Elm/Gleam; the mechanism requires both a registry hook (where to compare against) and a published-API extraction step that doesn't exist yet.

Track 2: Irreversible semantics

  • Language versioning and compatibility. The mechanism (editions, fixers, a compatibility promise) for when the language stops breaking. Until then it breaks freely, which is correct before a first release.
  • Exhaustive struct pattern opt-in. Struct pattern matching is partial by default: unmentioned fields are ignored. A !.. marker could opt into exhaustive field matching, so User{name:, age:, email:, !..} would become a compile error when User gains a field. This is the inverse of Rust, where .. opts out of exhaustive matching. It waits on real usage showing the need.

Track 3: Architecture to leave room for

  • A stable serialization format. The linked-IR image (ir.EncodeImage/DecodeImage) is the one serialized form today and carries no compatibility promise outside .nomic, which ir.FormatVersion versions. An object is the same format: one module encoded alone, whose symbols carry their linkage names, so objects, instances and images share one codec and one version. Front-end artifacts have a codec of their own beside it: a file's interface (analysis.FileInterface) writes its declarations' nodes with internal/ast/astcodec, generated from the AST's types, under its own version.
  • WASM Component Model interop for cross-language imports and exports. WIT interfaces and wasip2 components are the standard that would replace the wasip1 reactor's generic nomi_call ABI, which passes function names and JSON as data because one prebuilt runner serves every program and Go fixes a module's export names when it links it. Go cannot produce components yet. Track it; nothing is designed.

Track 4: Big but additive

  • Unified container type/value syntax. Tuples ((Int, String) ↔ (1, "x")) and anonymous structs ({a: Int} ↔ {a: 1}) already use one outer syntax for type and value; lists and maps do not (List<Int> vs [1, 2, 3]). Proposal: also accept [Int] and {String => Int} as type forms. Needs its own design.
  • Field-projection derive (derive Getters for T). For an interface whose functions are pure field projections (fn hour(value: self) -> Int), synthesize the trivial impl, which would remove boilerplate like std::calendar's DateParts/TimeParts impls. derive covers Equatable, Hashable, Comparable, Debug, Display, ToJson and FromJson today.
  • Opaque handles for exported functions. Every argument and result of an export fn crosses as JSON, so a value the host passes back unchanged is encoded and decoded on each call. A handle (a value that stays in the VM, referred to by an id) would matter for large values and values with no JSON form. Wait for a program that needs it.
  • Checked examples in stdlib /// comments. The generated reference renders a declaration's //! attached tests as runnable editors, and those are the stdlib's examples. A ```nomi block inside a /// comment is only highlighted: nothing parses, checks or runs it, so one can go stale unnoticed. Either check those blocks or settle that //! is the only example form.

Track 5: Standard library I/O and services

Where each item lives follows one rule. std holds what Go's standard library can back with no third-party code: std::fs, std::sql's vocabulary, later std::http over net/http. lib/ holds first-party modules that need third-party Go code or are opinionated layers over std: database drivers (lib/sql/sqlite), lib/sql/sqlkit, later an HTTP router or framework. Each lib/ module is its own module with its own go.mod, versioned with nomi's commits, tested by nomi's checks, and added by users with nomi add github.com/nomi-language/nomi/lib/....

What a program needs to talk to the world outside the VM. The items are in the agreed order. Items 1 and 2 and the subprocesses std::process now has share one stream type (Reader/Writer) and one test seam, and were designed together in the I/O design proposal (docs/design/io.md, not committed), which also sketches 3, 4, 5 and 7. Every item is backed by Go's standard library, so no program needs a Go toolchain to use it.

  • 2. The file system, the rest. std::fs, std::path and std::fs::testing exist (whole files with a WriteMode, lines and chunks, streams, directories, walks and globs, metadata, symlinks and modes, io.File with reads and writes at a position, fs.within over os.Root, temporary directories, an in-memory sandbox, a conformance suite, the browser's in-memory file system). Missing: a test group line that seals a test's real file calls. Paths use / on every system, Windows hosts accepting \ too.
  • 5. HTTP under Node. std::http, std::tls and std::net cover Go's HTTP packages (the internal/stdhttp package doc; internal/stdhttp/inventory.txt names each of Go's identifiers and what Nomi does with it). Missing: a js/wasm request run under Node, where Go's transport does not use fetch.

markdown:
---
title: Introduction
description: What Nomi is like, how to run it, and how it relates to Go, before the tour's first chapter.
---

The Language Tour covers the whole language, a chapter at a time, each
building on the one before. It assumes you program already; if you don't,
start with [First Steps](/learn/values/).

## Nomi at a glance

- **Static types.** Named functions write out their parameter types and any
  return type other than `Unit`. Bindings and lambdas infer their types.
- **Immutable values.** Bindings, structs and collections never change. To
  "modify" a value, you make a new one.
- **Functional style.** Functions are values, types can be sums of variants,
  and [`case`](/pattern-matching/) must cover every shape a value can take.
  Tail calls run in constant stack space.
- **Plain control flow.** `return`, `break`, `continue` and a postfix `?` are
  there when they make a function easier to read.
- **Explicit interfaces.** A type implements an interface with
  `impl Interface for Type`, or gets a generated implementation with
  `derive`.
- **Qualified calls.** A function is called through the type, interface or
  file that owns it: `User.rename(user)`, `String.length(name)`,
  `Display.to_string(value)`. There is no `user.rename()`.
- **Pipes.** `x |> f()` lets data flow read from top to bottom.
- **Structured concurrency.** Tasks are started inside a
  [`concurrent` block](/concurrency/), which keeps them scoped to it.
  Channels and context-style cancellation are built in.
- **App fields.** Configuration and dependencies live on one
  [app value](/app-fields/). A test can swap one with a line
  such as `with App.logger = ...`.
- **Web apps.** A server renders checked HTML templates, or serves a React
  or Vue build and its JSON API; [Frontends](/frontends/) compares the ways.
- **Built-in tests.** [`test` blocks](/testing/), assertions and `//!`
  examples are ordinary Nomi code, and `nomi test` runs them.

:::note[Design Status]
Nomi is very early. This site is the main place to try the language while the
design is still being worked out. Expressions, types, pattern matching,
imports, interfaces, derives, tests, collections and control flow are the most
used and tested parts. Concurrency, calling Go, and module management are
newer.
:::

## Running Nomi

[Installing Nomi](/tooling/install/) covers getting the `nomi` command.
Then:

```console
$ nomi run app.nomi           # run a program
$ nomi run --watch app.nomi   # run it again on every save
$ nomi test                   # run every test under the current directory
$ nomi test --watch           # run the tests again on every save
$ nomi                        # an interactive REPL
$ nomi build app.nomi         # write a standalone executable
```

`nomi build` writes one executable file that needs nothing else installed.
`--target` builds it for another platform. `nomi build --web` writes a web
page that runs the program in the browser, the way the examples on this site
run. [Building & Shipping](/building-and-shipping/) covers these and the other
ways to ship a program.

### The Nomi VM

Nomi compiles your program and runs it on its own virtual machine (VM), as
Lua and Python do. Each function becomes bytecode the first time it runs:

- `nomi run`, `nomi test` and the REPL run your program on it.
- `nomi build` puts it in the executable beside your program.
- You can edit most examples on this site, and they run on the VM in your
  browser.
- A Go application can embed it to load a Nomi program and call its
  functions.

## Where Go fits

Nomi is written in Go. It follows Go on practical matters: garbage
collection, builds for other platforms, shipping one file, formatting and
tooling, and dependencies. The language itself is different from Go.

- A Nomi module works like a Go module. It is a directory tree with a
  manifest, `nomi.toml`, and it is versioned and used as one unit. Inside a
  module, you import a file, and `pub` controls what other files can see.
  There are no packages.
- Nomi can [call Go code](/calling-go/) when you need a library the
  standard library doesn't have. You don't need Go installed: Nomi's own
  libraries that wrap Go come prebuilt, and for your own Go code `nomi`
  uses the `go` on your `PATH` or downloads the release it was built with.

The tour starts with [Bindings & Expressions](/bindings-and-expressions/).

---
title: Coming from Go
description: What carries over from Go to Nomi, what differs, and the same program written in both.
---

Much of Go carries over: static types with inference for locals, errors as
values rather than exceptions, structs, interfaces, backtick raw strings, one
formatter for all code, tasks and channels, and a single executable from
`nomi build`. Nomi programs can also [call Go packages](/calling-go/)
directly. What differs most: values never change, errors pass up with a
postfix `?`, and a type implements an interface by saying so.

The [cheat sheet](/cheat-sheet/) lists the rules in one place.

## Will trip you up

| Go | Nomi |
|---|---|
| `x := 1`, `var x int`, `x++` | `x = 1`, `x: Int = 1`. Nothing is mutable; a later `x = ...` binds the name again. |
| `func (s Shape) Area() int`, `s.Area()` | `fn area(shape: Shape) -> Int` in an `impl Shape` block, `Shape.area(s)`: there are no method calls on a value |
| An interface is satisfied implicitly | `impl Interface for Type` |
| `nil` | `None`, from `Option<T>` |
| `func f() (int, string)`, `n, s := f()` | `fn f() -> (Int, String)`, a tuple, and `(n, s) = f()`. Its items are also read as `t.first`, `t.second`, ... |
| `if err != nil { return err }` | A postfix `?` on a `Result` or `Option` |
| `switch x { case 1: .. }` | `case x`, then an arm per line such as `1 -> ..`, then `end`; it must cover every value |
| `defer f.Close()` | `defer Reader.close_quietly(r)` on the line after opening. It runs when its block ends, where Go's waits for the function to return, and the checker requires it for a resource. `defer on error` runs only when the function fails. |
| `for i, x := range xs { .. }`, `for cond { .. }` | `Iter` functions: `Iter.each`, `Iter.map`, `Iter.reduce`, `Iter.with_index`. A loop over no collection is recursion or `Iter.loop`. |
| `float64(x)` | `Int.to_float(x)`. Nomi's `x as T` converts nothing: it only states a type the value already fits (`[] as List<String>`) |
| `a / b` panics when `b` is 0, and an `int` wraps on overflow | `/` and `%` on two `Int`s take a `NonZeroInt` divisor, so the check for zero comes before the division: a literal other than 0 is one, and so is `b` after `if b == 0 then return ..`. An `Int` is exact at any size and never overflows. |
| `go f()`, `sync.WaitGroup` | `Task.spawn(fn -> f())` inside `concurrent` ... `end`, which waits for its tasks |
| Dependencies built in `main` and passed to handlers in a struct | `fn boot() -> Result<App, String>` builds an `App` struct before `main` runs, and any function reads a field as `App.db`, with nothing passed down. A test replaces one with `with App.db = ..`. See [App Fields](/app-fields/). |

## Spelled differently

| Go | Nomi |
|---|---|
| `[]int{1, 2}`, `map[string]int{"a": 1}` | `[1, 2]`, `{"a" => 1}` |
| `Point{X: 1}` | `Point{x: 1}` |
| An exported name starts with a capital | `pub` |
| A `[]Dog` is no `[]Speaker`; copy it in a loop | A `List<Dog>` passes where a `List<Speaker>` is expected, with nothing copied |
| `select` | `Channel.select([..])` |
| `fmt.Sprintf("%d items", n)` | `"${n} items"` |
| `decimal.RequireFromString("1.50")` from `shopspring/decimal` | `1.50d`, a `Decimal` literal, in the language: `0.1d + 0.2d == 0.3d`. See [Exact arithmetic with `Decimal`](/scalars-and-strings/#exact-arithmetic-with-decimal). |
| `func Map[T any](..)` | `fn map<T>(..)` |
| `_test.go` files | `test "name"` ... `end` blocks beside the code |
| `import "app/db/posts"`, then `posts.Find(1)` | `import db::posts`, then `posts.find(1)`; where `posts` is taken, `import db` imports the directory and `db::posts.find(1)` reaches the file, instead of an import alias |
| `mux.HandleFunc("GET /users/{id}", show)`, then `r.PathValue("id")` | `Route.to_with("GET /users/{id}", show)` with `fn show(Request, user: {id: Int}) -> Response`. The handler gets `user.id` already parsed, `/users/ann` gets a 404, and the pattern is checked when the program is. `Route"GET /users/{id}"` on its own has a `String` field, as `PathValue` returns. See [HTTP](/http/#handlers-and-routes) and [Frontends](/frontends/). |

## The same program

```go
func countWords(text string) map[string]int {
	counts := map[string]int{}
	for _, w := range strings.Fields(text) {
		counts[strings.ToLower(w)]++
	}
	return counts
}

func parsePort(s string) (int, error) {
	n, err := strconv.Atoi(s)
	if err != nil {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf("not a number: %s", s)
	}
	if n < 1 || n > 65535 {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf("out of range: %d", n)
	}
	return n, nil
}
```

```nomi-run
// FILE: words.nomi
fn count_words(text: String) -> Map<String, Int>
    text
    |> String.words()
    |> Iter.map(String.lowercase)
    |> Iter.frequencies()
end

fn parse_port(text: String) -> Result<Int, String>
    n =
        text
        |> String.to_int()
        |> Option.to_result("not a number: ${text}")?

    if n < 1 or n > 65535 then
        Err("out of range: ${n}")
    else
        Ok(n)
    end
end

// FILE: words_test.nomi
import words.{count_words, parse_port}

test "the same program"
    assert count_words("the The cat") == {"the" => 2, "cat" => 1}
    assert parse_port("8080") == Ok(8080)
    assert parse_port("x") == Err("not a number: x")
    assert parse_port("0") == Err("out of range: 0")
end
```
<!-- expect
ok the same program
test result: ok. 1 passed, 0 failed
-->

`Iter.frequencies` counts each value into a new map, where the Go loop
changes one map in place. `||` and `&&` are written `or` and `and`.

title: Coming from Go description: What carries over from Go to Nomi, what differs, and the same program written in both.

Much of Go carries over: static types with inference for locals, errors as values rather than exceptions, structs, interfaces, backtick raw strings, one formatter for all code, tasks and channels, and a single executable from nomi build. Nomi programs can also call Go packages directly. What differs most: values never change, errors pass up with a postfix ?, and a type implements an interface by saying so.

The cheat sheet lists the rules in one place.

Will trip you up

Go Nomi
x := 1, var x int, x++ x = 1, x: Int = 1. Nothing is mutable; a later x = ... binds the name again.
func (s Shape) Area() int, s.Area() fn area(shape: Shape) -> Int in an impl Shape block, Shape.area(s): there are no method calls on a value
An interface is satisfied implicitly impl Interface for Type
nil None, from Option<T>
func f() (int, string), n, s := f() fn f() -> (Int, String), a tuple, and (n, s) = f(). Its items are also read as t.first, t.second, ...
if err != nil { return err } A postfix ? on a Result or Option
switch x { case 1: .. } case x, then an arm per line such as 1 -> .., then end; it must cover every value
defer f.Close() defer Reader.close_quietly(r) on the line after opening. It runs when its block ends, where Go's waits for the function to return, and the checker requires it for a resource. defer on error runs only when the function fails.
for i, x := range xs { .. }, for cond { .. } Iter functions: Iter.each, Iter.map, Iter.reduce, Iter.with_index. A loop over no collection is recursion or Iter.loop.
float64(x) Int.to_float(x). Nomi's x as T converts nothing: it only states a type the value already fits ([] as List<String>)
a / b panics when b is 0, and an int wraps on overflow / and % on two Ints take a NonZeroInt divisor, so the check for zero comes before the division: a literal other than 0 is one, and so is b after if b == 0 then return ... An Int is exact at any size and never overflows.
go f(), sync.WaitGroup Task.spawn(fn -> f()) inside concurrent ... end, which waits for its tasks
Dependencies built in main and passed to handlers in a struct fn boot() -> Result<App, String> builds an App struct before main runs, and any function reads a field as App.db, with nothing passed down. A test replaces one with with App.db = ... See App Fields.

Spelled differently

Go Nomi
[]int{1, 2}, map[string]int{"a": 1} [1, 2], {"a" => 1}
Point{X: 1} Point{x: 1}
An exported name starts with a capital pub
A []Dog is no []Speaker; copy it in a loop A List<Dog> passes where a List<Speaker> is expected, with nothing copied
select Channel.select([..])
fmt.Sprintf("%d items", n) "${n} items"
decimal.RequireFromString("1.50") from shopspring/decimal 1.50d, a Decimal literal, in the language: 0.1d + 0.2d == 0.3d. See Exact arithmetic with Decimal.
func Map[T any](..) fn map<T>(..)
_test.go files test "name" ... end blocks beside the code
import "app/db/posts", then posts.Find(1) import db::posts, then posts.find(1); where posts is taken, import db imports the directory and db::posts.find(1) reaches the file, instead of an import alias
mux.HandleFunc("GET /users/{id}", show), then r.PathValue("id") Route.to_with("GET /users/{id}", show) with fn show(Request, user: {id: Int}) -> Response. The handler gets user.id already parsed, /users/ann gets a 404, and the pattern is checked when the program is. Route"GET /users/{id}" on its own has a String field, as PathValue returns. See HTTP and Frontends.

The same program

func countWords(text string) map[string]int {
	counts := map[string]int{}
	for _, w := range strings.Fields(text) {
		counts[strings.ToLower(w)]++
	}
	return counts
}

func parsePort(s string) (int, error) {
	n, err := strconv.Atoi(s)
	if err != nil {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf("not a number: %s", s)
	}
	if n < 1 || n > 65535 {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf("out of range: %d", n)
	}
	return n, nil
}

// FILE: words.nomi
fn count_words(text: String) -> Map<String, Int>
    text
    |> String.words()
    |> Iter.map(String.lowercase)
    |> Iter.frequencies()
end

fn parse_port(text: String) -> Result<Int, String>
    n =
        text
        |> String.to_int()
        |> Option.to_result("not a number: ${text}")?

    if n < 1 or n > 65535 then
        Err("out of range: ${n}")
    else
        Ok(n)
    end
end

// FILE: words_test.nomi
import words.{count_words, parse_port}

test "the same program"
    assert count_words("the The cat") == {"the" => 2, "cat" => 1}
    assert parse_port("8080") == Ok(8080)
    assert parse_port("x") == Err("not a number: x")
    assert parse_port("0") == Err("out of range: 0")
end

Iter.frequencies counts each value into a new map, where the Go loop changes one map in place. || and && are written or and and.

--- title: Pipes description: The `|>` operator passes a value through a series of calls, so code reads from top to bottom. --- `x |> f()` means `f(x)`. The value on the left becomes the first argument of the call on the right. Pipes let you write a series of calls from top to bottom, instead of nesting them inside each other. Most Nomi code is written this way. ## The pipe operator ```nomi-run fn double(x: Int) -> Int x * 2 end fn add(x: Int, y: Int) -> Int x + y end fn main() 5 |> double() |> dbg 5 |> add(3) |> dbg end ``` When the call takes more arguments, you write the rest in the parentheses. `5 |> add(3)` is `add(5, 3)`.

Fine print

- A stage is a call. `5 |> double` is ``a pipe stage is a call: write `double()` ``, since a name without parentheses is a function value. - A lambda or a capture is a stage only after `then` or `tap`. `5 |> fn n -> n * 2` is an error that suggests `then`. - A variant stage names its enum: `5 |> Shape.Dot()`. A bare `.Dot()` works only where the pipeline's type is expected, as in `s: Shape = 5 |> .Dot()`. - `|> if` and `|> case` may prefix the call that computes their operand: `input |> case parse_id()` is `input |> parse_id() |> case`, each above the same arms. Spec: [Pipes](/spec/expressions/#pipes), [Keyword stages](/spec/expressions/#keyword-stages).
A longer pipeline puts one stage on each line: ```nomi-run fn main() [1, 2, 3] |> Iter.map(fn n -> n * n) |> Iter.to_list() |> dbg end ``` ## Pipes start from data A pipeline reads best when it starts with the data and ends where the result is used. Here is the same calculation written both ways: ```nomi-run fn main() // inside-out dbg Iter.count(Iter.filter([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], &(&1 > 2))) // pipeline [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] |> Iter.filter(&(&1 > 2)) |> Iter.count() |> dbg end ``` Both give `3`. The nested version runs from the inside out, so you read it backwards. The pipeline runs in the order you read it. ## The `then` stage ```nomi-run fn main() " ada " |> String.trim() |> then fn name -> "Hello, ${name}!" |> dbg end ``` `then` calls a lambda, or a capture, with the piped value and passes on what it returns. Use it for a small step that no named function does. The lambda's body ends at the next `|>`, so the stages after it are still part of the pipeline.

Fine print

- A `then` capture may use `&1` more than once, positional or named. The piped value is computed once: `3 |> then &add(&1, b: &1)` is 6. - A second parameter is an error: the stage passes one value. - A lambda's parameter is out of scope after its body ends. Using it in a later stage is an error whose help says to write the body below the `->`, closed by `end`. ```nomi fn main() total = [3, 4] |> then fn xs -> xs |> Iter.map(&(&1 * 2)) |> Iter.sum() end |> then &(&1 + 1) dbg total // 15 end ``` Spec: [The `then` stage](/spec/expressions/#the-then-stage).
## Piping into another argument A call stage takes the piped value as its first argument. To pass it as another argument, write the `then` stage with a [capture](/functions-and-lambdas/#captures), whose `&1` is the piped value: ```nomi-run fn divide(x: Int, y: NonZeroInt) -> Int x / y end fn main() 10 |> then ÷(100, &1) |> dbg 100 |> then ÷(y: 4, x: &1) |> dbg end ``` `10 |> then ÷(100, &1)` is `divide(100, 10)`. A named argument can be `&1` too: `100 |> then ÷(y: 4, x: &1)` is `divide(100, 4)`. The stage passes one value, so the capture takes one parameter. A bare `&1` in a call stage, as in `10 |> divide(100, &1)`, is an error that suggests the `then` stage. ## The `tap` stage ```nomi-run import std::io fn main() shout = "go north now" |> String.words() |> tap fn words -> io.print("got ${Iter.count(words)} words") |> Iter.map(String.uppercase) |> String.join(" ") io.print(shout) end ``` `tap` calls a lambda with the piped value and then passes the same value on. Use it for a side effect, such as logging. The lambda must return `Unit`. A function works by name too: `|> tap io.print`. If a `tap` lambda returns some other value, the compiler reports an error and suggests `then`, because `tap` would throw that value away. To look at a value while debugging, a bare `dbg` stage is shorter. Use `tap` for effects the program keeps.

Fine print

- A `tap` body may end in `dbg`, as a `Unit` function body may. - A `?` inside the lambda exits the lambda, so its result is a `Result` or `Option`, not `Unit`, and the stage is rejected. - `tap?` is an error: `tap` passes its input on, so there is nothing for the `?` to propagate. Use `then?`. Spec: [The `tap` stage](/spec/expressions/#the-tap-stage).
## Other stages A bare `dbg` stage prints the value and passes it on. A stage that starts with `not` negates the stage's result: `name |> not String.is_empty()` is `not String.is_empty(name)`. A [`?`](/pattern-matching/#passing-failures-up) after a stage unwraps its [`Option`](/reference/option/) or [`Result`](/reference/results/). It passes on the value inside a `Some` or an `Ok`. On `None` or `Err`, it returns that from the function straight away: ```nomi-run fn parse(text: String) -> Option text |> String.trim() |> String.to_int()? |> then &(&1 * 2) |> Some() end fn main() dbg parse(" 21 ") dbg parse("abc") end ``` When a `then` lambda's result is what can fail, write `then?`: `|> then? fn n -> half(n)` passes on the value inside, or returns the `None` or `Err` from the function. An [assertion](/testing/#assertions) can check the result of a whole pipeline: ```nomi-run test "pipeline result is true" assert " Ada Lovelace " |> String.trim() |> String.contains("Ada") end ``` `if` and `case` can take the piped value as well. Here the value becomes the first argument of `String.contains`, the call that computes the `if` condition. The `case` matches its arms against the piped value: ```nomi-run fn main() "Ada" |> if String.contains("A") then "initialed" else "plain" end |> dbg Some("Ada") |> case Some(name) -> "named ${name}" None -> "missing" end |> dbg end ``` ## See it in action
Word CountCount each word in a sentence. AcronymBuild an acronym from a phrase. High ScoresThe latest, the best and the top three.
Every example that uses Pipes [Scalars & Strings](/scalars-and-strings/) is next.

x |> f() means f(x). The value on the left becomes the first argument of the call on the right. Pipes let you write a series of calls from top to bottom, instead of nesting them inside each other. Most Nomi code is written this way.

The pipe operator

fn double(x: Int) -> Int
    x * 2
end

fn add(x: Int, y: Int) -> Int
    x + y
end

fn main()
    5 |> double() |> dbg

    5 |> add(3) |> dbg
end

When the call takes more arguments, you write the rest in the parentheses. 5 |> add(3) is add(5, 3).

  • A stage is a call. 5 |> double is a pipe stage is a call: write `double()` , since a name without parentheses is a function value.
  • A lambda or a capture is a stage only after then or tap. 5 |> fn n -> n * 2 is an error that suggests then.
  • A variant stage names its enum: 5 |> Shape.Dot(). A bare .Dot() works only where the pipeline's type is expected, as in s: Shape = 5 |> .Dot().
  • |> if and |> case may prefix the call that computes their operand: input |> case parse_id() is input |> parse_id() |> case, each above the same arms.

Spec: Pipes, Keyword stages.

A longer pipeline puts one stage on each line:

fn main()
    [1, 2, 3]
    |> Iter.map(fn n -> n * n)
    |> Iter.to_list()
    |> dbg
end

Pipes start from data

A pipeline reads best when it starts with the data and ends where the result is used. Here is the same calculation written both ways:

fn main()
    // inside-out
    dbg Iter.count(Iter.filter([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], &(&1 > 2)))

    // pipeline
    [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
    |> Iter.filter(&(&1 > 2))
    |> Iter.count()
    |> dbg
end

Both give 3. The nested version runs from the inside out, so you read it backwards. The pipeline runs in the order you read it.

The then stage

fn main()
    "  ada  "
    |> String.trim()
    |> then fn name -> "Hello, ${name}!"
    |> dbg
end

then calls a lambda, or a capture, with the piped value and passes on what it returns. Use it for a small step that no named function does. The lambda's body ends at the next |>, so the stages after it are still part of the pipeline.

  • A then capture may use &1 more than once, positional or named. The piped value is computed once: 3 |> then &add(&1, b: &1) is 6.
  • A second parameter is an error: the stage passes one value.
  • A lambda's parameter is out of scope after its body ends. Using it in a later stage is an error whose help says to write the body below the ->, closed by end.
fn main()
    total =
        [3, 4]
        |> then fn xs ->
            xs |> Iter.map(&(&1 * 2)) |> Iter.sum()
        end
        |> then &(&1 + 1)

    dbg total // 15
end

Spec: The then stage.

Piping into another argument

A call stage takes the piped value as its first argument. To pass it as another argument, write the then stage with a capture, whose &1 is the piped value:

fn divide(x: Int, y: NonZeroInt) -> Int
    x / y
end

fn main()
    10 |> then &divide(100, &1) |> dbg
    100 |> then &divide(y: 4, x: &1) |> dbg
end

10 |> then &divide(100, &1) is divide(100, 10). A named argument can be &1 too: 100 |> then &divide(y: 4, x: &1) is divide(100, 4). The stage passes one value, so the capture takes one parameter. A bare &1 in a call stage, as in 10 |> divide(100, &1), is an error that suggests the then stage.

The tap stage

import std::io

fn main()
    shout =
        "go north now"
        |> String.words()
        |> tap fn words -> io.print("got ${Iter.count(words)} words")
        |> Iter.map(String.uppercase)
        |> String.join(" ")

    io.print(shout)
end

tap calls a lambda with the piped value and then passes the same value on. Use it for a side effect, such as logging. The lambda must return Unit. A function works by name too: |> tap io.print.

If a tap lambda returns some other value, the compiler reports an error and suggests then, because tap would throw that value away. To look at a value while debugging, a bare dbg stage is shorter. Use tap for effects the program keeps.

  • A tap body may end in dbg, as a Unit function body may.
  • A ? inside the lambda exits the lambda, so its result is a Result or Option, not Unit, and the stage is rejected.
  • tap? is an error: tap passes its input on, so there is nothing for the ? to propagate. Use then?.

Spec: The tap stage.

Other stages

A bare dbg stage prints the value and passes it on. A stage that starts with not negates the stage's result: name |> not String.is_empty() is not String.is_empty(name).

A ? after a stage unwraps its Option or Result. It passes on the value inside a Some or an Ok. On None or Err, it returns that from the function straight away:

fn parse(text: String) -> Option<Int>
    text
    |> String.trim()
    |> String.to_int()?
    |> then &(&1 * 2)
    |> Some()
end

fn main()
    dbg parse("  21  ")
    dbg parse("abc")
end

When a then lambda's result is what can fail, write then?: |> then? fn n -> half(n) passes on the value inside, or returns the None or Err from the function.

An assertion can check the result of a whole pipeline:

test "pipeline result is true"
    assert "  Ada Lovelace  "
        |> String.trim()
        |> String.contains("Ada")
end

if and case can take the piped value as well. Here the value becomes the first argument of String.contains, the call that computes the if condition. The case matches its arms against the piped value:

fn main()
    "Ada"
    |> if String.contains("A") then
        "initialed"
    else
        "plain"
    end
    |> dbg

    Some("Ada")
    |> case
        Some(name) -> "named ${name}"
        None       -> "missing"
    end
    |> dbg
end
