--- title: "Money" description: "Amounts of money with std::money: writing them, adding them, rounding them, custom currencies, showing them to a reader, and reading prices people type." --- [`std::money`](/reference/money/) has `Money`, an amount in a currency. The amount is a `Decimal`, so it is exact. The currency is a [`Currency`](/reference/currency/) from `std::currency`. ## Writing an amount `Money"19.99 USD"` is an amount of US dollars: the amount, one space and the currency's ISO 4217 code. Interpolating a `Money` writes the same text. Both fields are public, so when the amount comes from a variable, build the value from its fields with `Money{...}`: ```nomi-run import std::currency.Currency std::io std::money.Money end fn main() price = Money"19.99 USD" io.print(price) dbg price.amount dbg price.currency cents = 1999 amount = Int.to_decimal(cents) / 100d dbg Money{amount:, currency: Currency"USD"} == price end ``` The compiler checks a `Money` literal, so a missing currency, an unknown code or a malformed amount is an error before the program runs: ```nomi-run error import std::money.Money fn main() price = Money"19.99" dbg price end ``` `Money.parse("19.99 EUR")` reads the same text while the program runs, and returns that error as a value. The amount keeps every digit you write, as a `Decimal` does. `Money"12.5 USD"` and `Money"12.50 USD"` are equal, but only the second has two digits after the point. ## Adding amounts `*` multiplies an amount by an `Int`. Adding and subtracting are functions that return a `Result`, since dollars and euros don't add: `Money.add` and `Money.subtract` take two amounts, and `Money.sum` adds a list of them. It takes the currency too, so the sum of an empty list is zero in that currency. Nothing is lost to rounding: ```nomi-run import std::currency.Currency std::io std::money.{CurrencyMismatch, Money} end fn main() -> Result book = Money"12.50 USD" pen = Money"2.35 USD" io.print(Money.add(book, pen)?) io.print(Money.subtract(book, pen)?) io.print(book * 3) io.print(Money.sum([book, pen, pen], Currency"USD")?) empty: List = [] io.print(Money.sum(empty, Currency"USD")?) Ok(Unit) end ``` ## Mixing currencies Adding dollars to euros gives a number with no meaning, so it is an `Err(CurrencyMismatch)`, which names both currencies. Here `main` passes it on with `?`, and the program stops with it: ```nomi-run error import std::io std::money.{CurrencyMismatch, Money} end fn main() -> Result price = Money"12.50 USD" fee = Money"2.00 EUR" total = Money.add(price, fee)? io.print(total) Ok(Unit) end ``` Convert one amount first, with a rate your program gets from somewhere it trusts. Where the currencies are known to match, as for two literals, write `!` after the call instead of `?`. `Money.min` and `Money.max` return a `Result` the same way. ## Rounding `Money` keeps every digit until you round it. A third of $10.00 is $3.333333 to six places, and it stays that way through more arithmetic. `Money.round` rounds an amount to its currency's digits: two for the dollar, none for the yen. ```nomi-run import std::io std::money.Money end fn main() total = Money"10.00 USD" third = {..total, amount: .. |> Decimal.divide(3d, 6, .HalfEven)} io.print(third) io.print(Money.round(third)) io.print(Money.round(Money"0.125 USD")) io.print(Money.round(Money"0.135 USD")) io.print(Money.round(Money"0.125 USD", mode: .HalfUp)) io.print(Money.round(Money"1234.5 JPY")) end ``` A tie, an amount exactly halfway like `0.125`, rounds to the even digit by default: `0.12`, and `0.135` to `0.14`. Rounding every tie up would make a long list of rounded amounts add up to a little more than the exact total. Rounding to even sends half the ties down and half up, so the errors cancel out. Pass `mode:` for another rule, such as `.HalfUp`, when a law or a contract asks for it. Three rounded thirds of $10.00 make $9.99, so a bill split that way loses a cent. `Money.split` gives parts that sum to the amount exactly, the leftover cent going to the first part, and `Money.allocate` splits by ratios: ```nomi-run import std::io std::money.Money end fn main() io.print(Money.split(Money"10.00 USD", 3)) io.print(Money.allocate(Money"10.00 USD", [70, 30])) end ``` A plain `Decimal` splits the same way, to the number of digits you name: `Decimal.split(100d, 3, 2)` is `[33.34d, 33.33d, 33.33d]`, and `Decimal.allocate` takes ratios. ## Custom currencies A shop may count in something that isn't money in a bank, such as loyalty points. A custom currency has its own code and says how many digits it has after the point: `PTS:0` has none. A module lists the custom currencies it writes in its `nomi.toml`, in the `[money]` section, and then writes them in `Currency` and `Money` literals the same way. A currency built from text the program reads while it runs needs no listing. This example is a small project of two files; each tab is one file: ```nomi-run // FILE: main.nomi import std::currency.Currency std::io std::money.Money end fn main() points = Money.add(Money"1200 PTS:0", Money"300 PTS:0")! io.print(points) io.print(Money.format(points, Locale"en-US")) dbg Currency.parse("PTS:0") == Ok(points.currency) end // FILE: nomi.toml [package] name = "shop" entry_points = ["main"] [money] custom_currencies = ["PTS:0"] ``` Two custom currencies are equal when their codes and digits are, so two libraries that each write `PTS:0` share one currency. `PTS:0` and `PTS:2` are two currencies, and adding them is an `Err`. A custom currency can't reuse an ISO code, and has no symbol, so `Money.format` writes its code. A custom currency needs no other setup, so the list is what catches a typo. A literal naming a custom currency the module doesn't list is an error when the program is checked, and it suggests a listed one that is close. With `PTS:0` listed, `Money"5 PST:0"` is: ```console error: typed literal Money"5 PST:0": `PST:0` is a custom currency this module does not list: add it to [money].custom_currencies in nomi.toml --> main.nomi:7:14 | 7 | io.print(Money"5 PST:0") | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ = help: did you mean `PTS:0`? nomi.toml lists it ```

The custom currency list

- `Currency.custom("PST", 0)` with both arguments written out is checked the same way as a literal. - Each module has its own list: a library lists the currencies it writes, and the application's list doesn't cover them. - A single file with no `nomi.toml`, like the other examples on this page, may write any custom currency. - [`[money]`](/tooling/projects/#money) lists what an entry may hold, and [`std::currency`](/reference/currency/) what a custom currency can do.
## Showing an amount to a reader `Money.format` writes a price the way a reader of a locale expects, with the currency's symbol in the right place. How a locale writes numbers is in [Locales & Formatting](/locales-and-formatting/). ```nomi-run import std::io std::money.Money end fn main() price = Money"1299.5 USD" [Locale"en-US", Locale"de", Locale"fr"] |> Iter.each(fn locale -> io.print("${locale}: ${Money.format(price, locale)}")) dbg "${price}" dbg Money.format(Money"1500 JPY", Locale"ja") end ``` The dollar sign comes before the amount in American English and after it in German and French. French writes `$US`, since several countries call their money a dollar. CLDR also knows how many digits each currency has after the decimal point. The dollar has two, so `1299.5` becomes `1,299.50`. The yen has none. Putting a `Money` in a string, as in `"${price}"`, gives the amount and the code: `1299.5 USD`, the text its literal is written in. Like a number in a string, it is the same for every reader. ### Showing the currency `display:` picks how the currency is shown: its symbol (the default), its narrow symbol, its code, or its name. ```nomi-run import std::money.Money fn main() usd = Money"5 USD" dbg Money.format(usd, Locale"en-US", display: .Code) dbg Money.format(usd, Locale"en-CA") end ``` After `USD` is a no-break space, which `dbg` writes `\u{a0}`. Canadian English writes `US$` for the US dollar, since `$` alone would mean the Canadian dollar. `display: .Narrow` writes `$5.00`, for a page where the currency is clear, and `.Name` writes `5.00 US dollars`. A [custom currency](#custom-currencies) has no symbol or name in CLDR, so it is always shown by its code. ## Reading what people type `Money.parse_in` reads a price a person typed, written the way their locale writes prices, in the currency you name. By default the price must have the currency's symbol or code where the locale puts it. `lenient: True` also takes the amount alone. ```nomi-run import std::currency.Currency std::money.Money end fn main() usd = Currency"USD" dbg Money.parse_in("$1,299.50", Locale"en-US", usd) dbg Money.parse_in("1299.50", Locale"en-US", usd, lenient: True) dbg Money.parse_in("€12.50", Locale"en-US", usd) end ``` A price in another currency is an error, and so is one with more digits than the currency has: `$12.505` is `Err(TooManyFractionDigits{max: 2})`. [Locales & Formatting](/locales-and-formatting/#reading-what-people-type) covers how each locale writes numbers, and the rest of what strict and lenient reading accept. ## Room for libraries `Money` holds only an amount and a currency, with both fields public, so payment, invoicing and accounting libraries can share one type. Std has no exchange rates. A library that has them takes a `Money`, checks its `currency`, and returns a new `Money` in the other currency, rounded with `Money.round` when it is ready to charge. [Locales & Formatting](/locales-and-formatting/) is next. It writes an amount, and numbers, dates and lists, the way a reader's language writes them.

title: "Money" description: "Amounts of money with std::money: writing them, adding them, rounding them, custom currencies, showing them to a reader, and reading prices people type."

std::money has Money, an amount in a currency. The amount is a Decimal, so it is exact. The currency is a Currency from std::currency.

Writing an amount

Money"19.99 USD" is an amount of US dollars: the amount, one space and the currency's ISO 4217 code. Interpolating a Money writes the same text. Both fields are public, so when the amount comes from a variable, build the value from its fields with Money{...}:

import
    std::currency.Currency
    std::io
    std::money.Money
end

fn main()
    price = Money"19.99 USD"
    io.print(price)
    dbg price.amount
    dbg price.currency

    cents = 1999
    amount = Int.to_decimal(cents) / 100d
    dbg Money{amount:, currency: Currency"USD"} == price
end

The compiler checks a Money literal, so a missing currency, an unknown code or a malformed amount is an error before the program runs:

import std::money.Money

fn main()
    price = Money"19.99"
    dbg price
end

Money.parse("19.99 EUR") reads the same text while the program runs, and returns that error as a value.

The amount keeps every digit you write, as a Decimal does. Money"12.5 USD" and Money"12.50 USD" are equal, but only the second has two digits after the point.

Adding amounts

* multiplies an amount by an Int. Adding and subtracting are functions that return a Result, since dollars and euros don't add: Money.add and Money.subtract take two amounts, and Money.sum adds a list of them. It takes the currency too, so the sum of an empty list is zero in that currency. Nothing is lost to rounding:

import
    std::currency.Currency
    std::io
    std::money.{CurrencyMismatch, Money}
end

fn main() -> Result<Unit, CurrencyMismatch>
    book = Money"12.50 USD"
    pen = Money"2.35 USD"

    io.print(Money.add(book, pen)?)
    io.print(Money.subtract(book, pen)?)
    io.print(book * 3)
    io.print(Money.sum([book, pen, pen], Currency"USD")?)

    empty: List<Money> = []
    io.print(Money.sum(empty, Currency"USD")?)
    Ok(Unit)
end

Mixing currencies

Adding dollars to euros gives a number with no meaning, so it is an Err(CurrencyMismatch), which names both currencies. Here main passes it on with ?, and the program stops with it:

import
    std::io
    std::money.{CurrencyMismatch, Money}
end

fn main() -> Result<Unit, CurrencyMismatch>
    price = Money"12.50 USD"
    fee = Money"2.00 EUR"
    total = Money.add(price, fee)?
    io.print(total)
    Ok(Unit)
end

Convert one amount first, with a rate your program gets from somewhere it trusts. Where the currencies are known to match, as for two literals, write ! after the call instead of ?. Money.min and Money.max return a Result the same way.

Rounding

Money keeps every digit until you round it. A third of $10.00 is $3.333333 to six places, and it stays that way through more arithmetic. Money.round rounds an amount to its currency's digits: two for the dollar, none for the yen.

import
    std::io
    std::money.Money
end

fn main()
    total = Money"10.00 USD"
    third = {..total, amount: .. |> Decimal.divide(3d, 6, .HalfEven)}
    io.print(third)
    io.print(Money.round(third))

    io.print(Money.round(Money"0.125 USD"))
    io.print(Money.round(Money"0.135 USD"))
    io.print(Money.round(Money"0.125 USD", mode: .HalfUp))
    io.print(Money.round(Money"1234.5 JPY"))
end

A tie, an amount exactly halfway like 0.125, rounds to the even digit by default: 0.12, and 0.135 to 0.14. Rounding every tie up would make a long list of rounded amounts add up to a little more than the exact total. Rounding to even sends half the ties down and half up, so the errors cancel out. Pass mode: for another rule, such as .HalfUp, when a law or a contract asks for it.

Three rounded thirds of $10.00 make $9.99, so a bill split that way loses a cent. Money.split gives parts that sum to the amount exactly, the leftover cent going to the first part, and Money.allocate splits by ratios:

import
    std::io
    std::money.Money
end

fn main()
    io.print(Money.split(Money"10.00 USD", 3))
    io.print(Money.allocate(Money"10.00 USD", [70, 30]))
end

A plain Decimal splits the same way, to the number of digits you name: Decimal.split(100d, 3, 2) is [33.34d, 33.33d, 33.33d], and Decimal.allocate takes ratios.

Custom currencies

A shop may count in something that isn't money in a bank, such as loyalty points. A custom currency has its own code and says how many digits it has after the point: PTS:0 has none.

A module lists the custom currencies it writes in its nomi.toml, in the [money] section, and then writes them in Currency and Money literals the same way. A currency built from text the program reads while it runs needs no listing.

This example is a small project of two files; each tab is one file:

// FILE: main.nomi
import
    std::currency.Currency
    std::io
    std::money.Money
end

fn main()
    points = Money.add(Money"1200 PTS:0", Money"300 PTS:0")!
    io.print(points)
    io.print(Money.format(points, Locale"en-US"))
    dbg Currency.parse("PTS:0") == Ok(points.currency)
end

// FILE: nomi.toml
[package]
name = "shop"
entry_points = ["main"]

[money]
custom_currencies = ["PTS:0"]

Two custom currencies are equal when their codes and digits are, so two libraries that each write PTS:0 share one currency. PTS:0 and PTS:2 are two currencies, and adding them is an Err. A custom currency can't reuse an ISO code, and has no symbol, so Money.format writes its code.

A custom currency needs no other setup, so the list is what catches a typo. A literal naming a custom currency the module doesn't list is an error when the program is checked, and it suggests a listed one that is close. With PTS:0 listed, Money"5 PST:0" is:

error: typed literal Money"5 PST:0": `PST:0` is a custom currency this module does not list: add it to [money].custom_currencies in nomi.toml
 --> main.nomi:7:14
  |
7 |     io.print(Money"5 PST:0")
  |              ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = help: did you mean `PTS:0`? nomi.toml lists it
  • Currency.custom("PST", 0) with both arguments written out is checked the same way as a literal.
  • Each module has its own list: a library lists the currencies it writes, and the application's list doesn't cover them.
  • A single file with no nomi.toml, like the other examples on this page, may write any custom currency.
  • [money] lists what an entry may hold, and std::currency what a custom currency can do.

Showing an amount to a reader

Money.format writes a price the way a reader of a locale expects, with the currency's symbol in the right place. How a locale writes numbers is in Locales & Formatting.

import
    std::io
    std::money.Money
end

fn main()
    price = Money"1299.5 USD"

    [Locale"en-US", Locale"de", Locale"fr"]
    |> Iter.each(fn locale -> io.print("${locale}: ${Money.format(price, locale)}"))

    dbg "${price}"
    dbg Money.format(Money"1500 JPY", Locale"ja")
end

The dollar sign comes before the amount in American English and after it in German and French. French writes $US, since several countries call their money a dollar. CLDR also knows how many digits each currency has after the decimal point. The dollar has two, so 1299.5 becomes 1,299.50. The yen has none.

Putting a Money in a string, as in "${price}", gives the amount and the code: 1299.5 USD, the text its literal is written in. Like a number in a string, it is the same for every reader.

Showing the currency

display: picks how the currency is shown: its symbol (the default), its narrow symbol, its code, or its name.

import std::money.Money

fn main()
    usd = Money"5 USD"
    dbg Money.format(usd, Locale"en-US", display: .Code)
    dbg Money.format(usd, Locale"en-CA")
end

After USD is a no-break space, which dbg writes \u{a0}. Canadian English writes US$ for the US dollar, since $ alone would mean the Canadian dollar. display: .Narrow writes $5.00, for a page where the currency is clear, and .Name writes 5.00 US dollars. A custom currency has no symbol or name in CLDR, so it is always shown by its code.

Reading what people type

Money.parse_in reads a price a person typed, written the way their locale writes prices, in the currency you name. By default the price must have the currency's symbol or code where the locale puts it. lenient: True also takes the amount alone.

import
    std::currency.Currency
    std::money.Money
end

fn main()
    usd = Currency"USD"
    dbg Money.parse_in("$1,299.50", Locale"en-US", usd)
    dbg Money.parse_in("1299.50", Locale"en-US", usd, lenient: True)
    dbg Money.parse_in("€12.50", Locale"en-US", usd)
end

A price in another currency is an error, and so is one with more digits than the currency has: $12.505 is Err(TooManyFractionDigits{max: 2}). Locales & Formatting covers how each locale writes numbers, and the rest of what strict and lenient reading accept.

Room for libraries

Money holds only an amount and a currency, with both fields public, so payment, invoicing and accounting libraries can share one type. Std has no exchange rates. A library that has them takes a Money, checks its currency, and returns a new Money in the other currency, rounded with Money.round when it is ready to charge.

Locales & Formatting is next. It writes an amount, and numbers, dates and lists, the way a reader's language writes them.

--- title: "Pattern Matching, Option & Result" description: "`case` takes values apart by shape. Option and Result hold a result or its absence, and `?` passes a failure up." --- A `case` expression takes a value and runs the first arm whose pattern matches it. You saw simple `case` expressions in [Bindings & Expressions](/bindings-and-expressions/). This chapter covers more kinds of pattern, then [`Option`](/reference/option/), [`Result`](/reference/results/), and the `?` that passes a failure up. A `case` must cover every possible value. If you leave out a variant of an enum, the program does not compile. You find out when you build, not when the program runs. ## Binding patterns and guards ```nomi-run fn label(text: String) -> String case String.length(text) 0 -> "empty" n when n > 10 -> "long, ${n} characters" n -> "${n} characters" end end fn main() dbg label("") dbg label("hello") dbg label("hello there, world") end ``` Each arm starts its own line. An arm whose `->` ends its line takes the lines below as its body, up to the next arm or the `case`'s `end`. A plain name in a pattern, like `n`, matches any value and gives it that name, here the length. `when` adds a condition, called a guard. The arm runs only if the condition is true. `_` matches anything and names nothing.

Fine print

- An arm with a guard never counts toward covering every value, since its condition may be false. - Literal patterns never cover their type: no list of numbers or strings covers `Int` or `String`, so `label` needs its last arm. - Coverage works part by part. For a pair of `Option` values, arms for `(Some(x), _)` and `(_, Some(y))` miss `non-exhaustive case on (Option, Option): missing (None, None)`. - A literal never converts: `3` doesn't match a `Float`. Write `3.0`. Spec: [Exhaustiveness checking](/spec/patterns/#exhaustiveness-checking), [Guards](/spec/patterns/#guards), [Literal patterns](/spec/patterns/#literal-patterns).
## Destructuring Patterns can also take a value apart. This is the `Shape` enum from [Structs, Enums, Distinct Types](/structs-enums-distinct/): ```nomi-run enum Shape Circle Float Rectangle {width: Float, height: Float} end fn area(s: Shape) -> Float case s .Circle(r) -> r * r * 3.14159 .Rectangle{width:, height:} -> width * height end end fn main() dbg area(.Circle(3.0)) dbg area(.Rectangle{width: 4.0, height: 5.0}) end ``` `.Circle(r)` matches a circle and names its radius `r`. `.Rectangle{width:, height:}` matches a rectangle and names both fields. Tuples and structs work the same way: `(a, b) -> ...` and `Point{x:, y:} -> ...`. A pattern is written the way the value is built. ### Lists, vectors and sets A bracket pattern takes apart the list, vector or set it matches. Over a list or a vector it names items from the front, `..` stands for the rest, and items after the `..` are named from the end. Over a set it checks which values the set holds: ```nomi-run fn first_two(words: List) -> String case words [] -> "no words" [only] -> only [a, b, ..] -> "${a} ${b}" end end fn last(v: Vector) -> Option case v [] -> None [.., z] -> Some(z) end end fn access(roles: Set) -> String case roles ["admin", ..] -> "everything" ["editor", "viewer", ..] -> "write and read" _ -> "read only" end end fn main() dbg first_two(["hello", "big", "world"]) dbg last([1, 2, 3]) dbg access(["viewer", "editor"]) dbg access(["viewer"]) end ``` `[a, b, ..]` matches a list of two or more items and ignores the rest; `..rest` would name it. `[.., z]` matches a vector of at least one item and names the last, and `["graph {", ..body, "}"]` names the lines between two others. Reaching a list's last items walks the list once. The compiler checks list and vector arms by length, so `first_two` and `last` need no `_` arm. Over a set, the pattern matches when the set holds every value it lists, in any order. `..others` names the values it did not list, and without a `..` the set must hold exactly the values written. The values are constants, looked up rather than bound, so a set pattern can never cover every set, and `access` needs its `_` arm. The arguments need no `Vector` or `Set`: each parameter's type says which collection `[...]` is. A string pattern can match a prefix: the arm `"/users/" + id -> ...` matches a string that starts with `/users/` and names the rest `id`.

Fine print

- A map pattern, `{"port" => p}`, matches a map that holds every key it names; other keys are ignored. A missing key just fails to match. Like a set pattern, it needs a `_` arm. - Map keys and set elements are values to look up, never names to bind: `[_, ..]` over a set is an error. A set's elements are constants, and a guard tests a value in scope: `[..] when Set.contains(roles, role)`. - In a string prefix pattern the left side is a plain string literal and the right side a name. The rest may be empty, and the pattern can nest: `Some("/users/" + id)`. - A list pattern takes one `..`. Items before it match from the front, and items after it from the end. ```nomi fn route(path: String) -> String case path "/users/" + id -> "user ${id}" "/health" -> "ok" _ -> "not found" end end ``` Spec: [Map Destructuring](/spec/patterns/#map-destructuring), [Set Destructuring](/spec/patterns/#set-destructuring), [String Prefix Patterns](/spec/patterns/#string-prefix-patterns), [List Destructuring](/spec/patterns/#list-destructuring).
### Naming the whole match with `as` Sometimes an arm needs both the parts and the whole value. `pattern as name` matches the pattern and also gives the whole value a name: ```nomi-run enum Shape Circle Float Rectangle {width: Float, height: Float} end fn area(s: Shape) -> Float case s .Circle(r) -> r * r * 3.0 .Rectangle{width:, height:} -> width * height end end fn describe(s: Shape) -> String case s .Rectangle{width:, height:} as sq when width == height -> "a square of area ${area(sq)}" other -> "a shape of area ${area(other)}" end end fn main() dbg describe(.Rectangle{width: 2.0, height: 2.0}) dbg describe(.Circle(1.0)) end ``` The first arm reads `width` and `height`, and passes the whole rectangle to `area` as `sq`. Without `as`, it would have to build the rectangle again. `as` names the whole pattern to its left. `Ok(x) as r` names the whole `Result`. `Ok(Point{x:, y:} as p)` names only the `Point` inside. The name has the type of the value it names, so `sq` is a `Shape`. `as` works anywhere a pattern does, including `if`, bindings, parameters and inside other patterns. After a value in an expression, `as` states a type instead ([Type annotations](/bindings-and-expressions/#type-annotations)).

Fine print

- `as` binds looser than `or`: `A or B as x` names the value whichever alternative matched. To name one alternative, use parentheses: `(A as a) or B`. - The pattern doesn't narrow the name: `Ok(_) as r` over a `Result` binds a `Result`. - It must add a name: `_ as x` is an error that asks for `x`. - A guard's names come from the pattern, and the guard applies to the whole arm. Spec: [Naming the Whole Match](/spec/patterns/#naming-the-whole-match-as), [Alternatives](/spec/patterns/#alternatives-or).
### Matching alternatives with `or` `A or B` matches a value that either pattern matches, so one arm can handle several shapes: ```nomi-run enum Shape Circle Float Square Float Rectangle {width: Float, height: Float} end fn size(s: Shape) -> String case s .Circle(r) or .Square(r) when r > 10.0 -> "big, ${r} across" .Circle(r) or .Square(r) -> "${r} across" .Rectangle{width:, height:} -> "${width} by ${height}" end end fn main() dbg size(.Square(12.0)) dbg size(.Circle(2.0)) end ``` Every alternative must bind the same names, with the same types. Here both bind `r` as a `Float`, and `r` holds the value from whichever one matched. The `when` guard applies to the whole arm: if it is false, matching goes on to the next arm. `or` works inside other patterns too, as in `Some(.Circle(_) or .Square(_))`. A trailing `as` names the whole value whichever alternative matched. Together, the alternatives count toward covering every value, so `.Red or .Green` and `.Blue` cover a three-color enum without `_`. ### Testing a match with `is` `value is Pattern` asks whether a value matches a pattern. It is a `Bool` and binds nothing, so it fits wherever a condition does, in place of a `case` with a `True` arm and a `_ -> False` arm: ```nomi-run enum Block Item String Text String end fn closes(c: Codepoint) -> Bool c is (')' or ']' or '}') end fn main() blocks = [Block.Item("milk"), .Text("note"), .Item("eggs")] dbg blocks |> Iter.count_by(&(&1 is .Item(_))) dbg closes(']') dbg not Some(3) is None end ``` An `or` pattern after `is` goes in parentheses, since a bare `or` there joins two `Bool`s. A name in the pattern is an error: to use the payload, bind it with a `case` or with `if Some(n) = x`, as [`Option` and `Result`](#optiont-and-resultt-e) shows. ## `Option` and `Result` Nomi uses two enums for operations that might not have a result: - [`Option`](/reference/option/) is either `Some(value)` or `None`. Use it when there may be no result and there is nothing more to say about why. - [`Result`](/reference/results/) is either `Ok(value)` or `Err(error)`. Use it when a failure comes with an error that explains it. Both types and their variants are always available. You do not import them. ```nomi-run fn lookup(id: Int) -> Option case id 1 -> Some("Alice") 2 -> Some("Bob") _ -> None end end fn name_for(id: Int) -> String case lookup(id) Some(name) -> name None -> "unknown" end end fn main() dbg name_for(1) dbg name_for(99) end ``` For a quick check of a single pattern, `if` can match it directly. The names the pattern binds exist only in the first branch: ```nomi-run fn lookup(id: Int) -> Option case id 1 -> Some("Alice") _ -> None end end fn label_for(id: Int) -> String if Some(name) = lookup(id) then name else "unknown" end end fn main() dbg label_for(1) dbg label_for(9) end ``` ## Passing failures up ```nomi-run fn safe_div(a: Int, b: Int) -> Result if b == 0 then Err("div by zero") else Ok(a / b) end fn calculate(x: Int, y: Int) -> Result half = safe_div(x, 2)? ratio = safe_div(half, y)? Ok(ratio + 1) end fn main() dbg calculate(100, 5) dbg calculate(100, 0) end ``` A `?` after an `Option` or `Result` value gives you the value inside, or returns the `None` or `Err` from the whole function at once. The function must return the same kind: an `Option`'s `?` needs a function that returns an `Option`. To turn one into the other, use `Option.to_result`, as below. When the `Err`'s type is not the function's error type, `?` applies that type's `From` impl ([spec](/spec/failure/#propagating-with-)). In `calculate(100, 0)`, the second `safe_div` fails, so `calculate` returns `Err("div by zero")` and never reaches `Ok(ratio + 1)`. `main` can return `Result`, and then you can use `?` in it: ```nomi-run error fn safe_div(a: Int, b: Int) -> Result if b == 0 then Err("div by zero") else Ok(a / b) end fn calculate(x: Int, y: Int) -> Result half = safe_div(x, 2)? ratio = safe_div(half, y)? Ok(ratio + 1) end fn main() -> Result ratio = calculate(100, 0)? dbg ratio Ok(Unit) end ``` This `main` prints `error: div by zero` to stderr and exits with status 1. That is what happens whenever `main` returns an `Err`. The error is printed with `Display` if its type has it, so a `String` prints as itself. Otherwise it is printed with `Debug`. `main` must return either nothing or a `Result`. Any other return type is a compile error, because nothing would use the value. To show a value, print it with `io.print` and return `Ok(Unit)`. To exit with a status other than 1, make `E` an `Exit` from `std::process` and return it in an `Err`, as [Input & Output](/input-and-output/#exit-codes) shows. Inside a lambda, a `?` returns from the lambda, not from the function around it, just as `return` does. To parse a list of inputs, map each one to a `Result` and end the pipe with `Result.collect()?`: ```nomi-run fn parse(text: String) -> Result Option.to_result(String.to_int(text), "not a number: ${text}") end fn total(inputs: List) -> Result numbers = inputs |> Iter.map(parse) |> Result.collect()? Ok(Iter.sum(numbers)) end fn main() dbg total(["1", "2", "3"]) dbg total(["1", "x", "y"]) (numbers, errors) = ["1", "x", "y"] |> Iter.map(parse) |> Result.partition() dbg numbers dbg errors end ``` `Result.collect` gives the list of values when every input parsed. Otherwise it gives the first `Err`, and stops reading at that input. When you want every error, not just the first, `Result.partition` splits the results into two lists: the values and the errors. For `Option`, `Option.collect` gives `Some` of every value or `None`, and `Option.values` keeps the `Some` values and drops the rest. An `Option` is also an `Iter` of zero or one elements, so it goes where an `Iter` does: `Iter.to_list(Some(3))` is `[3]`, `Iter.to_list(None)` is `[]`, and `Iter.flat_map` with a function that returns an `Option` keeps only the `Some` values.

Fine print

- `?` converts an error only through a `From` impl. With none, an `Err` of another type is an error that suggests converting first: `status(text) |> Result.map_err(fn code -> "error ${code}")?`. - `?` binds as tightly as a call: `load()?.name` reads `name` from the loaded value. - A `?` can't stand directly in a `once` initializer or a default value. There is no function for it to return from. - In a test body, a failing `?` ends the test and reports the value. Spec: [Propagating with `?`](/spec/failure/#propagating-with-).
## Binding with `else` `?` passes a failure up. Sometimes you want to handle it right where it happens instead. Write the pattern you expect, then `else` and what to do when the value does not match: ```nomi-run enum PortError Missing Invalid String end fn parse_port(text: Option) -> Result Some(raw) = text else return Err(.Missing) Some(n) = String.to_int(raw) else return Err(.Invalid(raw)) Ok(n) end fn port(text: Option) -> Result Ok(n) = parse_port(text) else Err(.Missing) -> 8080 Err(.Invalid(raw)) -> return Err("bad port: ${raw}") end Ok(n) end fn main() dbg port(Some("3000")) dbg port(Some("eighty")) dbg port(None) end ``` When the value matches, the names in the pattern can be used for the rest of the block. When it does not, the `else` part runs. On the `else`'s own line it is a value or a jump. On the lines below, closed by `end`, it is statements, or `case` arms over the value that did not match. `parse_port` writes it on the `else`'s line. Each one returns an error. `port` uses `case` arms over the error that came back. A missing port gives `8080`, which takes the place of the `Ok` value, so `n` is `8080`. An invalid port returns an error naming the bad text. Each path through the `else` must do one of two things. It can leave, with `return` (or `break` or `continue` inside a loop callback). Or it can give a value to use in place of the matched one, as `8080` does for `n`. That works only when the pattern binds a single value. `[first, ..rest] = xs else ...` binds two, so its `else` must leave.

Fine print

- The pattern's names are not in scope inside the `else`. - A path that traps, with `unreachable "..."` or `todo`, counts as leaving. - A fallback stands in for one variant's payload. A nested pattern such as `Ok(Some(x))` has no single payload, so its `else` must leave. - A pattern that always matches takes no `else`: `(x, y) = pair else return` is `this pattern always matches; remove the else`. Spec: [Bindings with `else`](/spec/patterns/#bindings-with-else).
## Calls that cannot fail A `!` written right after an expression unwraps its `Option` or `Result`: ```nomi-run error fn half(n: Int) -> Result if n % 2 == 0 then Ok(n / 2) else Err("${n} is odd") end end fn main() ages = {"Ada" => 36, "Grace" => 45} dbg Map.get(ages, "Ada")! dbg half(10)! dbg "8" |> String.to_int()! dbg Map.get(ages, "Alan")! end ``` `Map.get(ages, "Ada")!` is `36`, not `Some(36)`. When the value is `None` or `Err`, the program stops at that line and quotes the expression. A `None` says it found nothing, as above, and an `Err` shows the error: `half(3)!` stops with ``line 12: `half(3)` failed: 3 is odd``. Use `!` when a failure would be a bug in your own code: the arguments are constants, the key came from the map itself, or the input was checked already. When the failure can really happen, pass it up with `?` or handle it with `case` or `else`. `!` works on any expression that is an `Option` or a `Result`: a call, a pipe stage (`"8" |> String.to_int()!`), a field (`user.nickname!`) or a name. ## What can fail at run time A Nomi program stops while it runs in two ways: it asks to, or it hits a limit. It asks with a `!`, an [`unreachable`](/functions-and-lambdas/#code-that-cannot-be-reached) or a [`todo`](/functions-and-lambdas/#unwritten-code), or by awaiting a task that [failed](/concurrency/#when-a-task-fails). The limits are few. A program can run out of memory, make more than 100,000 nested calls, ask for a `Decimal` with more than about two billion digits after the point, or ask `String.repeat` for more than 2 GiB of text. A pipeline that consumes the whole of an endless iterator stops with a message instead of hanging ([Iter](/collections/#iter)). A program can also never finish. The checks happen where values enter, so the operations after them cannot fail: - A value that must meet a rule has a [refinement](/structs-enums-distinct/#refinements): a count is a `NonNegativeInt`, a list with a first element a `NonEmptyList`. - A literal passed where a refinement is expected is checked when the program compiles. - A check narrows a binding: after `if d == 0 then return ...`, `d` is a `NonZeroInt`. The compiler also follows ranges, so each `d` in `1..=n` is one too, and `Int.modulo(n, 26)` and `Int.clamp(n, 0..=9)` are `NonNegativeInt`s. - `/` and `%` take a `NonZeroInt` divisor ([Numbers](/scalars-and-strings/#numbers-booleans-operators)), so a division by zero does not compile. - A lookup that may miss returns an [`Option`](#optiont-and-resultt-e), and an operation that fails for a reason returns a `Result`. ```nomi-run fn average(total: Int, count: Int) -> Option if count == 0 then return None Some(total / count) end fn divisors(n: Int) -> List 1..=n |> Iter.filter(fn d -> n % d == 0) |> Iter.to_list() end fn main() dbg average(17, 4) dbg average(17, 0) dbg divisors(12) end ``` Without the check, `average` does not compile: ```nomi-run error fn average(total: Int, count: Int) -> Int total / count end fn main() dbg average(17, 4) end ``` The compiler proves a divisor is not zero from the checks and ranges already in the code, with no solver and nothing to annotate. Other languages draw these lines in other places: | | Nomi | Elm | Gleam | Rust | Go | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Integer division by zero | Compile error | Returns `0` | Returns `0` | Panic | Panic | | Index past the end | `Option` | `Option` | No indexing | Panic | Panic | | Integer overflow | None | Target decides | None on Erlang | Debug panic, release wraps | Wraps | | A failed task | Trap when awaited | Typed error | Linked processes crash | `Err` from `join` | Panic ends the program | - **Nomi** has no `xs[i]`: `Vector.get` and `Iter.get` return an `Option`, and an `Int` has no size limit. A task that returns an `Err` has not failed; that is its result. A task fails when its body traps. Every task is waited on, and how you wait decides: `Task.await` traps with the same fault, and `Task.outcome` returns the failure as a value. - **Elm**'s `//` returns `0`, but `modBy 0 n` crashes. Its integers are exact within 32 bits; past that the compilation target decides. - **Gleam**'s `/` returns `0`, and the separate function `int.divide` returns an `Error` instead. On JavaScript its `Int` is a 64-bit float. A process affects no other unless they are linked: `process.spawn` links the new process to its parent, and `process.spawn_unlinked` does not. - **Rust**'s `v[i]` panics and `get` returns an `Option`. - **Go** refuses a constant zero divisor when compiling. - **Calling the host language:** in Nomi a Go `error` arrives as a `Result`, and a Go panic stops the calling task. Elm has no direct calls, only flags and ports. A Gleam external's type is trusted, and a wrong one can crash at run time. Write `!` where you know a fact the types cannot see, such as a key that came from the map itself. Each place a program can stop is then written in its source. ## See it in action

title: "Pattern Matching, Option & Result" description: "case takes values apart by shape. Option and Result hold a result or its absence, and ? passes a failure up."

A case expression takes a value and runs the first arm whose pattern matches it. You saw simple case expressions in Bindings & Expressions. This chapter covers more kinds of pattern, then Option<T>, Result<T, E>, and the ? that passes a failure up.

A case must cover every possible value. If you leave out a variant of an enum, the program does not compile. You find out when you build, not when the program runs.

Binding patterns and guards

fn label(text: String) -> String
    case String.length(text)
        0             -> "empty"
        n when n > 10 -> "long, ${n} characters"
        n             -> "${n} characters"
    end
end

fn main()
    dbg label("")
    dbg label("hello")
    dbg label("hello there, world")
end

Each arm starts its own line. An arm whose -> ends its line takes the lines below as its body, up to the next arm or the case's end.

A plain name in a pattern, like n, matches any value and gives it that name, here the length. when adds a condition, called a guard. The arm runs only if the condition is true. _ matches anything and names nothing.

  • An arm with a guard never counts toward covering every value, since its condition may be false.
  • Literal patterns never cover their type: no list of numbers or strings covers Int or String, so label needs its last arm.
  • Coverage works part by part. For a pair of Option<Int> values, arms for (Some(x), _) and (_, Some(y)) miss non-exhaustive case on (Option<Int>, Option<Int>): missing (None, None).
  • A literal never converts: 3 doesn't match a Float. Write 3.0.

Spec: Exhaustiveness checking, Guards, Literal patterns.

Destructuring

Patterns can also take a value apart. This is the Shape enum from Structs, Enums, Distinct Types:

enum Shape
    Circle Float
    Rectangle {width: Float, height: Float}
end

fn area(s: Shape) -> Float
    case s
        .Circle(r)                  -> r * r * 3.14159
        .Rectangle{width:, height:} -> width * height
    end
end

fn main()
    dbg area(.Circle(3.0))
    dbg area(.Rectangle{width: 4.0, height: 5.0})
end

.Circle(r) matches a circle and names its radius r. .Rectangle{width:, height:} matches a rectangle and names both fields.

Tuples and structs work the same way: (a, b) -> ... and Point{x:, y:} -> .... A pattern is written the way the value is built.

Lists, vectors and sets

A bracket pattern takes apart the list, vector or set it matches. Over a list or a vector it names items from the front, .. stands for the rest, and items after the .. are named from the end. Over a set it checks which values the set holds:

fn first_two(words: List<String>) -> String
    case words
        []         -> "no words"
        [only]     -> only
        [a, b, ..] -> "${a} ${b}"
    end
end

fn last(v: Vector<Int>) -> Option<Int>
    case v
        []      -> None
        [.., z] -> Some(z)
    end
end

fn access(roles: Set<String>) -> String
    case roles
        ["admin", ..]            -> "everything"
        ["editor", "viewer", ..] -> "write and read"
        _                        -> "read only"
    end
end

fn main()
    dbg first_two(["hello", "big", "world"])
    dbg last([1, 2, 3])
    dbg access(["viewer", "editor"])
    dbg access(["viewer"])
end

[a, b, ..] matches a list of two or more items and ignores the rest; ..rest would name it. [.., z] matches a vector of at least one item and names the last, and ["graph {", ..body, "}"] names the lines between two others. Reaching a list's last items walks the list once. The compiler checks list and vector arms by length, so first_two and last need no _ arm.

Over a set, the pattern matches when the set holds every value it lists, in any order. ..others names the values it did not list, and without a .. the set must hold exactly the values written. The values are constants, looked up rather than bound, so a set pattern can never cover every set, and access needs its _ arm. The arguments need no Vector or Set: each parameter's type says which collection [...] is.

A string pattern can match a prefix: the arm "/users/" + id -> ... matches a string that starts with /users/ and names the rest id.

  • A map pattern, {"port" => p}, matches a map that holds every key it names; other keys are ignored. A missing key just fails to match. Like a set pattern, it needs a _ arm.
  • Map keys and set elements are values to look up, never names to bind: [_, ..] over a set is an error. A set's elements are constants, and a guard tests a value in scope: [..] when Set.contains(roles, role).
  • In a string prefix pattern the left side is a plain string literal and the right side a name. The rest may be empty, and the pattern can nest: Some("/users/" + id).
  • A list pattern takes one ... Items before it match from the front, and items after it from the end.
fn route(path: String) -> String
    case path
        "/users/" + id -> "user ${id}"
        "/health"      -> "ok"
        _              -> "not found"
    end
end

Spec: Map Destructuring, Set Destructuring, String Prefix Patterns, List Destructuring.

Naming the whole match with as

Sometimes an arm needs both the parts and the whole value. pattern as name matches the pattern and also gives the whole value a name:

enum Shape
    Circle Float
    Rectangle {width: Float, height: Float}
end

fn area(s: Shape) -> Float
    case s
        .Circle(r)                  -> r * r * 3.0
        .Rectangle{width:, height:} -> width * height
    end
end

fn describe(s: Shape) -> String
    case s
        .Rectangle{width:, height:} as sq when width == height -> "a square of area ${area(sq)}"
        other -> "a shape of area ${area(other)}"
    end
end

fn main()
    dbg describe(.Rectangle{width: 2.0, height: 2.0})
    dbg describe(.Circle(1.0))
end

The first arm reads width and height, and passes the whole rectangle to area as sq. Without as, it would have to build the rectangle again.

as names the whole pattern to its left. Ok(x) as r names the whole Result. Ok(Point{x:, y:} as p) names only the Point inside. The name has the type of the value it names, so sq is a Shape.

as works anywhere a pattern does, including if, bindings, parameters and inside other patterns. After a value in an expression, as states a type instead (Type annotations).

  • as binds looser than or: A or B as x names the value whichever alternative matched. To name one alternative, use parentheses: (A as a) or B.
  • The pattern doesn't narrow the name: Ok(_) as r over a Result<Int, String> binds a Result<Int, String>.
  • It must add a name: _ as x is an error that asks for x.
  • A guard's names come from the pattern, and the guard applies to the whole arm.

Spec: Naming the Whole Match, Alternatives.

Matching alternatives with or

A or B matches a value that either pattern matches, so one arm can handle several shapes:

enum Shape
    Circle Float
    Square Float
    Rectangle {width: Float, height: Float}
end

fn size(s: Shape) -> String
    case s
        .Circle(r) or .Square(r) when r > 10.0 -> "big, ${r} across"
        .Circle(r) or .Square(r)               -> "${r} across"
        .Rectangle{width:, height:}            -> "${width} by ${height}"
    end
end

fn main()
    dbg size(.Square(12.0))
    dbg size(.Circle(2.0))
end

Every alternative must bind the same names, with the same types. Here both bind r as a Float, and r holds the value from whichever one matched. The when guard applies to the whole arm: if it is false, matching goes on to the next arm.

or works inside other patterns too, as in Some(.Circle(_) or .Square(_)). A trailing as names the whole value whichever alternative matched. Together, the alternatives count toward covering every value, so .Red or .Green and .Blue cover a three-color enum without _.

Testing a match with is

value is Pattern asks whether a value matches a pattern. It is a Bool and binds nothing, so it fits wherever a condition does, in place of a case with a True arm and a _ -> False arm:

enum Block
    Item String
    Text String
end

fn closes(c: Codepoint) -> Bool
    c is (')' or ']' or '}')
end

fn main()
    blocks = [Block.Item("milk"), .Text("note"), .Item("eggs")]
    dbg blocks |> Iter.count_by(&(&1 is .Item(_)))
    dbg closes(']')
    dbg not Some(3) is None
end

An or pattern after is goes in parentheses, since a bare or there joins two Bools. A name in the pattern is an error: to use the payload, bind it with a case or with if Some(n) = x, as Option<T> and Result<T, E> shows.

Option<T> and Result<T, E>

Nomi uses two enums for operations that might not have a result:

  • Option<T> is either Some(value) or None. Use it when there may be no result and there is nothing more to say about why.
  • Result<T, E> is either Ok(value) or Err(error). Use it when a failure comes with an error that explains it.

Both types and their variants are always available. You do not import them.

fn lookup(id: Int) -> Option<String>
    case id
        1 -> Some("Alice")
        2 -> Some("Bob")
        _ -> None
    end
end

fn name_for(id: Int) -> String
    case lookup(id)
        Some(name) -> name
        None       -> "unknown"
    end
end

fn main()
    dbg name_for(1)
    dbg name_for(99)
end

For a quick check of a single pattern, if can match it directly. The names the pattern binds exist only in the first branch:

fn lookup(id: Int) -> Option<String>
    case id
        1 -> Some("Alice")
        _ -> None
    end
end

fn label_for(id: Int) -> String
    if Some(name) = lookup(id) then
        name
    else
        "unknown"
    end
end

fn main()
    dbg label_for(1)
    dbg label_for(9)
end

Passing failures up

fn safe_div(a: Int, b: Int) -> Result<Int, String>
    if b == 0 then Err("div by zero") else Ok(a / b)
end

fn calculate(x: Int, y: Int) -> Result<Int, String>
    half = safe_div(x, 2)?
    ratio = safe_div(half, y)?
    Ok(ratio + 1)
end

fn main()
    dbg calculate(100, 5)
    dbg calculate(100, 0)
end

A ? after an Option or Result value gives you the value inside, or returns the None or Err from the whole function at once. The function must return the same kind: an Option's ? needs a function that returns an Option. To turn one into the other, use Option.to_result, as below. When the Err's type is not the function's error type, ? applies that type's From impl (spec).

In calculate(100, 0), the second safe_div fails, so calculate returns Err("div by zero") and never reaches Ok(ratio + 1).

main can return Result<Unit, E>, and then you can use ? in it:

fn safe_div(a: Int, b: Int) -> Result<Int, String>
    if b == 0 then Err("div by zero") else Ok(a / b)
end

fn calculate(x: Int, y: Int) -> Result<Int, String>
    half = safe_div(x, 2)?
    ratio = safe_div(half, y)?
    Ok(ratio + 1)
end

fn main() -> Result<Unit, String>
    ratio = calculate(100, 0)?
    dbg ratio
    Ok(Unit)
end

This main prints error: div by zero to stderr and exits with status 1. That is what happens whenever main returns an Err. The error is printed with Display if its type has it, so a String prints as itself. Otherwise it is printed with Debug.

main must return either nothing or a Result<Unit, E>. Any other return type is a compile error, because nothing would use the value. To show a value, print it with io.print and return Ok(Unit).

To exit with a status other than 1, make E an Exit from std::process and return it in an Err, as Input & Output shows.

Inside a lambda, a ? returns from the lambda, not from the function around it, just as return does.

To parse a list of inputs, map each one to a Result and end the pipe with Result.collect()?:

fn parse(text: String) -> Result<Int, String>
    Option.to_result(String.to_int(text), "not a number: ${text}")
end

fn total(inputs: List<String>) -> Result<Int, String>
    numbers = inputs |> Iter.map(parse) |> Result.collect()?

    Ok(Iter.sum(numbers))
end

fn main()
    dbg total(["1", "2", "3"])
    dbg total(["1", "x", "y"])

    (numbers, errors) =
        ["1", "x", "y"]
        |> Iter.map(parse)
        |> Result.partition()

    dbg numbers
    dbg errors
end

Result.collect gives the list of values when every input parsed. Otherwise it gives the first Err, and stops reading at that input.

When you want every error, not just the first, Result.partition splits the results into two lists: the values and the errors. For Option, Option.collect gives Some of every value or None, and Option.values keeps the Some values and drops the rest.

An Option is also an Iter of zero or one elements, so it goes where an Iter does: Iter.to_list(Some(3)) is [3], Iter.to_list(None) is [], and Iter.flat_map with a function that returns an Option keeps only the Some values.

  • ? converts an error only through a From impl. With none, an Err of another type is an error that suggests converting first: status(text) |> Result.map_err(fn code -> "error ${code}")?.
  • ? binds as tightly as a call: load()?.name reads name from the loaded value.
  • A ? can't stand directly in a once initializer or a default value. There is no function for it to return from.
  • In a test body, a failing ? ends the test and reports the value.

Spec: Propagating with ?.

Binding with else

? passes a failure up. Sometimes you want to handle it right where it happens instead. Write the pattern you expect, then else and what to do when the value does not match:

enum PortError
    Missing
    Invalid String
end

fn parse_port(text: Option<String>) -> Result<Int, PortError>
    Some(raw) = text else return Err(.Missing)

    Some(n) = String.to_int(raw) else return Err(.Invalid(raw))

    Ok(n)
end

fn port(text: Option<String>) -> Result<Int, String>
    Ok(n) = parse_port(text) else
        Err(.Missing)      -> 8080
        Err(.Invalid(raw)) -> return Err("bad port: ${raw}")
    end

    Ok(n)
end

fn main()
    dbg port(Some("3000"))
    dbg port(Some("eighty"))
    dbg port(None)
end

When the value matches, the names in the pattern can be used for the rest of the block. When it does not, the else part runs. On the else's own line it is a value or a jump. On the lines below, closed by end, it is statements, or case arms over the value that did not match.

parse_port writes it on the else's line. Each one returns an error.

port uses case arms over the error that came back. A missing port gives 8080, which takes the place of the Ok value, so n is 8080. An invalid port returns an error naming the bad text.

Each path through the else must do one of two things. It can leave, with return (or break or continue inside a loop callback). Or it can give a value to use in place of the matched one, as 8080 does for n. That works only when the pattern binds a single value. [first, ..rest] = xs else ... binds two, so its else must leave.

  • The pattern's names are not in scope inside the else.
  • A path that traps, with unreachable "..." or todo, counts as leaving.
  • A fallback stands in for one variant's payload. A nested pattern such as Ok(Some(x)) has no single payload, so its else must leave.
  • A pattern that always matches takes no else: (x, y) = pair else return is this pattern always matches; remove the else.

Spec: Bindings with else.

Calls that cannot fail

A ! written right after an expression unwraps its Option or Result:

fn half(n: Int) -> Result<Int, String>
    if n % 2 == 0 then
        Ok(n / 2)
    else
        Err("${n} is odd")
    end
end

fn main()
    ages = {"Ada" => 36, "Grace" => 45}
    dbg Map.get(ages, "Ada")!
    dbg half(10)!
    dbg "8" |> String.to_int()!
    dbg Map.get(ages, "Alan")!
end

Map.get(ages, "Ada")! is 36, not Some(36). When the value is None or Err, the program stops at that line and quotes the expression. A None says it found nothing, as above, and an Err shows the error: half(3)! stops with line 12: `half(3)` failed: 3 is odd.

Use ! when a failure would be a bug in your own code: the arguments are constants, the key came from the map itself, or the input was checked already. When the failure can really happen, pass it up with ? or handle it with case or else.

! works on any expression that is an Option or a Result: a call, a pipe stage ("8" |> String.to_int()!), a field (user.nickname!) or a name.

What can fail at run time

A Nomi program stops while it runs in two ways: it asks to, or it hits a limit.

It asks with a !, an unreachable or a todo, or by awaiting a task that failed.

The limits are few. A program can run out of memory, make more than 100,000 nested calls, ask for a Decimal with more than about two billion digits after the point, or ask String.repeat for more than 2 GiB of text. A pipeline that consumes the whole of an endless iterator stops with a message instead of hanging (Iter). A program can also never finish.

The checks happen where values enter, so the operations after them cannot fail:

  • A value that must meet a rule has a refinement: a count is a NonNegativeInt, a list with a first element a NonEmptyList.
  • A literal passed where a refinement is expected is checked when the program compiles.
  • A check narrows a binding: after if d == 0 then return ..., d is a NonZeroInt. The compiler also follows ranges, so each d in 1..=n is one too, and Int.modulo(n, 26) and Int.clamp(n, 0..=9) are NonNegativeInts.
  • / and % take a NonZeroInt divisor (Numbers), so a division by zero does not compile.
  • A lookup that may miss returns an Option, and an operation that fails for a reason returns a Result.
fn average(total: Int, count: Int) -> Option<Int>
    if count == 0 then return None
    Some(total / count)
end

fn divisors(n: Int) -> List<Int>
    1..=n
    |> Iter.filter(fn d -> n % d == 0)
    |> Iter.to_list()
end

fn main()
    dbg average(17, 4)
    dbg average(17, 0)
    dbg divisors(12)
end

Without the check, average does not compile:

fn average(total: Int, count: Int) -> Int
    total / count
end

fn main()
    dbg average(17, 4)
end

The compiler proves a divisor is not zero from the checks and ranges already in the code, with no solver and nothing to annotate.

Other languages draw these lines in other places:

Nomi Elm Gleam Rust Go
Integer division by zero Compile error Returns 0 Returns 0 Panic Panic
Index past the end Option Option No indexing Panic Panic
Integer overflow None Target decides None on Erlang Debug panic, release wraps Wraps
A failed task Trap when awaited Typed error Linked processes crash Err from join Panic ends the program
  • Nomi has no xs[i]: Vector.get and Iter.get return an Option, and an Int has no size limit. A task that returns an Err has not failed; that is its result. A task fails when its body traps. Every task is waited on, and how you wait decides: Task.await traps with the same fault, and Task.outcome returns the failure as a value.
  • Elm's // returns 0, but modBy 0 n crashes. Its integers are exact within 32 bits; past that the compilation target decides.
  • Gleam's / returns 0, and the separate function int.divide returns an Error instead. On JavaScript its Int is a 64-bit float. A process affects no other unless they are linked: process.spawn links the new process to its parent, and process.spawn_unlinked does not.
  • Rust's v[i] panics and get returns an Option.
  • Go refuses a constant zero divisor when compiling.
  • Calling the host language: in Nomi a Go error arrives as a Result, and a Go panic stops the calling task. Elm has no direct calls, only flags and ports. A Gleam external's type is trusted, and a wrong one can crash at run time.

Write ! where you know a fact the types cannot see, such as a key that came from the map itself. Each place a program can stop is then written in its source.

# postgres

The Postgres driver for Nomi's `std/sql`, written in Nomi: it speaks
Postgres's frontend/backend protocol (version 3) over `std::net` and
`std::tls`, so a program that uses it needs no Go toolchain, no C
compiler and no `libpq`. `postgres.pool(url)` returns a `Conn`, std/sql's
interface, so code written against `Conn` runs on it unchanged.

```sh
nomi add github.com/nomi-language/nomi/lib/sql/postgres
```

```nomi
import
    std::io
    std::sql.{self, Conn, Error, Row, Sql}
    postgres
end

fn main() -> Result<Unit, Error>
    db = postgres.pool("postgres://localhost/notes")
    defer sql.close_quietly(db)

    _ = Conn.exec(
        db,
        Sql"CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS notes (id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, body TEXT NOT NULL)",
    )?

    _ = Conn.exec(db, Sql"INSERT INTO notes (body) VALUES (${"hello"})")?
    rows = Conn.query(db, Sql"SELECT body FROM notes")?

    Iter.each(rows, fn row ->
        io.print(
            Row.get<String>(row, "body")
            |> Result.with_default("?")
        )
    end)

    Ok(Unit)
end
```

A program that uses the driver has the effects of `std::net` (it dials
the server), `std::tls` (when the connection is TLS), `std::channels`
(the pool's and each connection's state), `std::random` (the SCRAM nonce)
and `std::instant` (the pool's ages and the reads' deadlines);
`postgres.scratch()` adds `std::process`. `nomi effects --write` writes
them into a project's `[effects]` tables.

## What it does

- `postgres.pool(url)` is a pool of connections. It connects lazily: an
  unreachable server, or a URL that does not parse, is `Error.Connection`
  from the first statement, so a program that must fail early calls
  `Conn.ping`. A statement runs on any connection of the pool, and waits
  for one when all `pool_max_conns` (4 unless the URL says) are busy. A
  connection is dropped once it outlives `pool_max_conn_lifetime` (1 hour)
  or sits idle past `pool_max_conn_idle_time` (30 minutes), and one idle
  for over a second answers an empty query before a statement uses it.
- `postgres.connect(url)` is one connection, opened now. A temporary table
  lives on one connection, so code that uses one connects.
- The URL is `postgres://user:password@host:port/name?key=value` or libpq's
  `key=value` words. The keys are `host`, `port`, `user`, `password`,
  `dbname`, `sslmode` (`disable`, `allow`, `prefer`, the default,
  `require`, `verify-ca`, `verify-full`), `sslrootcert`, `sslcert`,
  `sslkey`, `connect_timeout` (seconds) and the pool's three; any other key
  is a setting each connection starts with (`application_name`,
  `search_path`, `client_encoding`).
- A password is sent as the server asks: SCRAM-SHA-256, MD5, or in clear.
- `Conn.begin_transaction` is `BEGIN` on a connection the transaction
  holds until it commits or rolls back; on a transaction it is a
  savepoint, which `commit` releases and `rollback` rolls back to. A
  statement must run on the innermost open transaction or savepoint, and
  the driver refuses one sent through an outer transaction.
- One `Conn` may be shared by every task of a program. On a pool, a
  statement from another task while a transaction is open runs on another
  connection. On a `connect` connection, it waits for the transaction to
  end and then runs outside it; inside the transaction, use the `Conn` its
  `begin` returned, since a statement through the connection would wait
  for its own transaction.
- Parameters are bound as `$1`, `$2`, ..., never spliced into the SQL. A
  statement is prepared the first time a connection runs its SQL and kept,
  so it runs in one round trip after that; a statement with no parameters
  given to `exec` is sent as a simple query, which may hold several
  statements, as a migration does.
- A task that is cancelled, or whose `Context.with_timeout` deadline
  passes, while a statement runs stops within a tenth of a second. The
  statement is cancelled on the server, and the connection stays usable:
  the next statement on it reads what the server still sent for the
  stopped one first.
- A constraint error names the constraint as Postgres does, with its table
  and columns. A not-null violation is named as Postgres 18 names it
  (`users_email_not_null`), which older servers do not report. A
  serialization failure or a deadlock is `Error.Serialization`; any other
  error is `Error.Database` with its SQLSTATE.
- `postgres.listen(url, channel)` is a `Listener` on a connection of its
  own: `Listener.wait` answers the next `Notification` sent on the
  channel (`NOTIFY` or `pg_notify`). `Listener.close` ends a `wait`
  running on another task with `Error.Closed`.
- `Listener.receiver(listener, supervisor)` is the listener's
  notifications as a channel, `Receiver<Result<Notification, Error>>`, so
  one can be an arm of `Channel.select` beside a timer:

  ```nomi
  notes = Listener.receiver(listener, App.workers)

  Channel.select([
      Arm.receive(notes, fn note -> handle(note)),
      Arm.after(Duration.seconds(30), fn -> poll()),
  ])
  ```

  A task under the supervisor, which an app creates in `boot`, runs
  `Listener.forward`, which a program can also run in a task of its own.
  The channel closes when the task ends: after `close`, when the task is
  cancelled (as the supervisor's drain does at shutdown), or after a
  connection failure, which arrives first as a last value, `Err(e)`. So
  `None` means the listener was closed or the program is stopping, and
  `Err` means the connection failed. While the channel is full the task
  looks every 200 milliseconds at whether the listener was closed, so
  `close` ends it even when nothing reads the channel.
- `postgres.scratch()` is the URL of a fresh empty database on a
  throwaway server, for tests. The first call in a process starts the
  server with the `initdb` and `postgres` on `PATH`, in a temporary
  directory, on a free local port, with `fsync` off; it stops and its
  directory is removed within a second of the process ending, however it
  ends. Each call makes another database on that server. Without `initdb`
  and `postgres` on `PATH`, or with no POSIX shell, it returns
  `Error.Connection` saying so.
- It passes `std/sql/testing`'s conformance suite (every rule;
  `postgres_test.nomi`).
- `postgres/describe` is what `nomi tool sqlkit generate` asks a Postgres
  database. `describe.describe(url, migrations, statements)` makes a
  scratch database, `nomi_prepare_<hash>_<random>`, on the development
  server at `url`, applies the migrations, and answers the tables, each
  statement's inferred parameter types and its result columns: their
  types, the table column each reads, and whether it may be NULL. A column
  is non-null only when it reads a `NOT NULL` column that no outer join of
  the statement can leave out, which the statement's generic plan shows
  (`EXPLAIN EXECUTE` under `plan_cache_mode = force_generic_plan`, so
  Postgres 12 or later). A view's column is described through the view's
  definition, as the table column that one reads. It drops the scratch
  database before it answers.
- In the browser (the tour's wasm build) std::net has no sockets, so every
  call answers `Error.Connection`.

## Values

| `Value` | Written as | Read back from |
|---|---|---|
| `Int` | its digits, as the type the server asks for; past 64 bits, a `BIGINT` refuses it and a `NUMERIC` takes it | `smallint`, `integer`, `bigint`, `oid` |
| `Float` | binary `float8` or `float4` | `real`, `double precision`; also `numeric`'s `NaN` and infinities |
| `Decimal` | its digits | `numeric` |
| `Text` | itself | `text`, `varchar`, `char`, `name`, and any type with no `Value` of its own (an interval, an enum, `inet`, `citext`), as its text |
| `Bool` | `true` or `false` | `boolean` |
| `Bytes` | binary `bytea` | `bytea` |
| `Date`, `Time`, `Timestamp`, `Timestamptz` | binary `date`, `time`, `timestamp`, `timestamptz` | the same; `infinity` and `-infinity` read as `Text` |
| `Uuid` | its text | `uuid` |
| `Json` | its text, to `json` or `jsonb` | `json`, `jsonb` |
| `Array` | an array literal of its elements, which must all be one kind | a one-dimensional array of any type above |

A `List<T>` is an `Array` parameter, so `WHERE id = ANY(${ids})` matches a
list of ids, and an array column reads as a `List<T>`
(`Row.get<List<Int>>`). A time keeps microseconds, as Postgres stores it.

## How it is built

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `postgres.nomi` | The public API: `pool`, `connect`, `scratch`, `listen`, `Listener`, and `Conn` for `PgConn`. |
| `config.nomi` | Connection strings, read into a `Config`. |
| `messages.nomi` | Each protocol message as bytes, and `decode` of the server's. |
| `auth.nomi` | SCRAM-SHA-256 and MD5, as functions from the server's message to the client's. |
| `types.nomi` | Each type's binary and text form, by OID. |
| `failures.nomi` | The `sql.Error` of each SQLSTATE. |
| `cell.nomi` | State several tasks share one at a time, which a stopped task never leaves taken. |
| `wire.nomi` | One connection: opening it, sending, reading, cancelling. |
| `session.nomi` | Statements on one connection: prepared, bound and executed, or simple. |
| `pooled.nomi` | The pool, its permits and idle connections, and transactions. |
| `scratch.nomi` | The throwaway server. |
| `describe.nomi` | What sqlkit asks of a schema. |

Everything but `wire.nomi`, `session.nomi`, `pooled.nomi`, `scratch.nomi`
and `describe.nomi` is pure, tested against recorded bytes and the RFCs'
examples.

## Not built

- `copy_from` (`COPY ... FROM STDIN`). It needs the driver's own
  connection behind a `Conn`, and a transaction's `Conn` reaches a program
  as the std interface, which offers no way back to it. A `COPY ... FROM
  STDIN` sent as a statement is refused with `Error.Database` coded
  `0A000`.
- Arrays of more than one dimension, and composite values, which are
  refused with a message.
- SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS: std::tls gives no channel-binding data.
  `sslmode=verify-ca` checks the server's host name too, as `verify-full`
  does.
- Unix-domain sockets, a URL naming several hosts, the `PG*` environment
  variables and `.pgpass`.
- `postgres.scratch()` on Windows.

## Tests

```sh
nomi test lib/sql/postgres
```

The tests run on `postgres.scratch()`'s throwaway server, so they need
`initdb` and `postgres` on `PATH`. Without them the tests fail, since a
Nomi test cannot skip itself; `TestLibModules` (`cmd/nomi`) skips this
module instead. `wire_test.nomi` answers a client's password with a server
written in the test, for each method, and `messages_test.nomi` and
`types_test.nomi` read recorded bytes.

# markdown Markdown for Nomi's `std/html`, over [goldmark](https://github.com/yuin/goldmark): `markdown.render(text)` is `text` rendered as HTML, an `Html` a template inserts as it is. ```sh nomi add github.com/nomi-language/nomi/lib/markdown ``` ```nomi import std::html.Html markdown end fn post(title: String, body: String) -> Html Html"""

${title}

${markdown.render(body)}
""" end ``` A release `nomi` carries the module's Go code prebuilt, so a program that uses it needs no Go toolchain while the module is at the release's commit, which `nomi add` takes and `nomi update` restores. Otherwise the Go code is built into the program's runner the first time a program that uses it runs, with the `go` on `PATH` or the Go toolchain `nomi` downloads. ## What it renders CommonMark, with GitHub's extensions: tables, strikethrough, task lists, and a bare URL as a link (`https://example.com` in a sentence). ## Why its output is trusted `render` answers its markup through `Html.trusted`, the one way into an `Html` that skips a template's escaping. It can, because goldmark's safe defaults are kept: - Text is escaped: `a < b` renders as `a < b`. - Raw HTML in the text is left out, written as ``. - A link or image whose URL has a dangerous scheme (`javascript:`) gets an empty URL. So Markdown a user wrote renders safely. There is no option to let raw HTML through.

Markdown for Nomi's std/html, over goldmark: markdown.render(text) is text rendered as HTML, an Html a template inserts as it is.

nomi add github.com/nomi-language/nomi/lib/markdown

import
    std::html.Html
    markdown
end

fn post(title: String, body: String) -> Html
    Html"""
        <article>
          <h1>${title}</h1>
          ${markdown.render(body)}
        </article>
        """
end

A release nomi carries the module's Go code prebuilt, so a program that uses it needs no Go toolchain while the module is at the release's commit, which nomi add takes and nomi update restores. Otherwise the Go code is built into the program's runner the first time a program that uses it runs, with the go on PATH or the Go toolchain nomi downloads.

What it renders

CommonMark, with GitHub's extensions: tables, strikethrough, task lists, and a bare URL as a link (https://example.com in a sentence).

Why its output is trusted

render answers its markup through Html.trusted, the one way into an Html that skips a template's escaping. It can, because goldmark's safe defaults are kept:

  • Text is escaped: a < b renders as a < b.
  • Raw HTML in the text is left out, written as <!-- raw HTML omitted -->.
  • A link or image whose URL has a dangerous scheme (javascript:) gets an empty URL.

So Markdown a user wrote renders safely. There is no option to let raw HTML through.

# Editor support

Each directory here is one editor's support for Nomi: `zed/`, `helix/`,
`nvim/`, `vscode/` and `bat/`. Each has its own README for users, except Zed,
whose setup is below. This file is the setup for running each editor against
this checkout while working on Nomi. The checklist after a grammar change,
publishing the grammar and the git hooks are in the repository's `AGENTS.md`
("Grammar and editor extensions"); the rules behind the grammar's checks are
in `tree-sitter-nomi/README.md`.

## All editors

`make dev-editors` (`scripts/dev-editors.sh`) installs `nomi` and `nomi lsp`
from this checkout, runs the Neovim and Helix dev setups, syncs Zed's grammar
checkout, says when Zed's dev extension must be reinstalled, and rebuilds and
installs the VS Code extension when `code` is on PATH. An editor that is not
installed is skipped; `make dev-nvim`, `make dev-helix` and `make dev-zed` run
one.

Every editor sends a module's `nomi.toml` to `nomi lsp` beside the `.nomi`
files, and keeps its own TOML highlighting for it: Zed sends every TOML
buffer, VS Code's client and Neovim's `root_dir` select `nomi.toml` by name,
and Helix's `nomi-catalog` language, over Helix's TOML grammar, globs it.
The server answers only a `nomi.toml` and a module's phrase catalogs.

The `post-merge` hook (`make enable-hooks`) runs the parts of that a merge
changed. It acts only on `main`, or on the branches listed in
`git config nomi.editorBranches` (space-separated, for example `main next`),
so agent worktrees, which share the clone's config, are unaffected.

## Zed

For a dev install Zed uses `editors/zed/grammars/nomi/` (gitignored) as the
grammar checkout. It requires that directory's `origin` to equal
`extension.toml`'s `repository`, tries `git fetch origin <rev>` (a failure is
ignored), then runs `git checkout <rev>`.

Run `scripts/sync-zed-grammar.sh` in any fresh clone or worktree, and after
grammar changes. It makes that directory a git repository with the published
origin whose `dev` branch holds this checkout's `tree-sitter-nomi/`. When the
pinned rev's files equal the local grammar, `extension.toml` is left alone;
otherwise the script points `rev` at the local commit and says so. Do not
commit that rev: `scripts/sync-zed-grammar.sh --restore` puts the committed
one back, and a publish overwrites it.

`languages/nomi/highlights.scm` is generated, by `make build-zed-queries`
(`scripts/sync-zed-highlights.sh`), from the canonical query
`tree-sitter-nomi/queries/highlights.scm`: the same patterns in reverse
order, because Zed gives a node the last pattern that captures it and
tree-sitter's highlighter the first, with five capture names renamed to
ones Zed's themes style. `attached-test-dim.scm`, beside the extension's
manifest, is the one part written by hand: the patterns that draw `//!`
attached tests as comments, which the generator places just under the `//!`
markers. Edit the canonical query or that file, never the generated one.
Helix's and Neovim's highlights are generated from Zed's, so `make
build-helix` and `make build-nvim` run this first.

Then run "zed: install dev extension" and select the `editors/zed/` directory
itself. Install the language server with `go install ./cmd/nomi lsp`; Zed
launches `nomi lsp` from PATH. `cargo test --manifest-path
editors/zed/Cargo.toml` tests the extension's task locator.

## Helix

`make dev-helix` links Helix's Nomi queries to this checkout and builds the
grammar from this checkout's `tree-sitter-nomi/`, so local grammar changes need
no publish. `make install-helix` copies a snapshot instead, for people who
only use Nomi. See `helix/README.md`.

## Neovim

Load `editors/nvim` from this checkout (lazy.nvim `dir =`) and run
`make dev-nvim` to compile `editors/nvim/parser/nomi.so`. `make install-nvim`
copies a snapshot into Neovim's package directory, for people who only use
Nomi. `make test-nvim` runs the plugin's headless checks. See `nvim/README.md`,
"Local development".

## VS Code

`make install-vscode` builds `editors/vscode/nomi.vsix` and installs it with
`code --install-extension`; never publish it to a marketplace.
`make test-vscode` runs its unit and grammar tests, and
`npm --prefix editors/vscode run test:smoke` runs the extension in a
downloaded VS Code. See `vscode/README.md`, "Working on the extension".

## bat

See `bat/README.md`, "Install for `bat`".

languages/nomi/highlights.scm is generated, by make build-zed-queries (scripts/sync-zed-highlights.sh), from the canonical query tree-sitter-nomi/queries/highlights.scm: the same patterns in reverse order, because Zed gives a node the last pattern that captures it and tree-sitter's highlighter the first, with five capture names renamed to ones Zed's themes style. attached-test-dim.scm, beside the extension's manifest, is the one part written by hand: the patterns that draw //! attached tests as comments, which the generator places just under the //! markers. Edit the canonical query or that file, never the generated one. Helix's and Neovim's highlights are generated from Zed's, so make build-helix and make build-nvim run this first.

Then run "zed: install dev extension" and select the editors/zed/ directory itself. Install the language server with go install ./cmd/nomi lsp; Zed launches nomi lsp from PATH. cargo test --manifest-path editors/zed/Cargo.toml tests the extension's task locator.

Helix

make dev-helix links Helix's Nomi queries to this checkout and builds the grammar from this checkout's tree-sitter-nomi/, so local grammar changes need no publish. make install-helix copies a snapshot instead, for people who only use Nomi. See helix/README.md.

Neovim

Load editors/nvim from this checkout (lazy.nvim dir =) and run make dev-nvim to compile editors/nvim/parser/nomi.so. make install-nvim copies a snapshot into Neovim's package directory, for people who only use Nomi. make test-nvim runs the plugin's headless checks. See nvim/README.md, "Local development".

VS Code

make install-vscode builds editors/vscode/nomi.vsix and installs it with code --install-extension; never publish it to a marketplace. make test-vscode runs its unit and grammar tests, and npm --prefix editors/vscode run test:smoke runs the extension in a downloaded VS Code. See vscode/README.md, "Working on the extension".
